choices: It means servers are located in a single data center for lower latency
It abstracts away undifferentiated infrastructure work so teams focus on their product
It removes the need for any on-premises hardware in every organization
It guarantees zero downtime for all hosted applications
evidence:
SRE team spent 3 sprints racking servers, patching
firmware, and replacing failed drives before the
app could ship. CTO asks: which cloud principle
would have eliminated this work?
scenarios.hint: What does AWS mean when it says you should stop doing 'undifferentiated heavy lifting'?
scenarios.prompt: Which statement best captures what 'going to the cloud' gives this team?
scenarios.situation: A startup's platform team spent three sprints racking servers, patching firmware, and replacing failed drives before their app could ship.
scenarios.title: The rack that shipped nothing
scenarios.why: The cloud's core value proposition is eliminating undifferentiated heavy lifting — racking, powering, cooling, and repairing physical infrastructure — so teams spend their time on the product. It does not mean one data center, zero hardware everywhere, or guaranteed zero downtime.

evidence:
Nov: 2k req/day baseline. Dec: 400k req/day spike.
Jan: back to 2k req/day. Provisioned fleet sat idle
for 11 months of the year.
scenarios.hint: The workload changed in both directions — what cloud benefit covers shrinking as well as growing?
scenarios.prompt: Which cloud benefit would have eliminated the idle-fleet cost?
scenarios.situation: An e-commerce shop provisions for its December peak all year: 2k requests/day normally, 400k/day in December, back to 2k in January.
scenarios.title: The December fleet
scenarios.why: Elasticity is the ability to scale capacity up AND down automatically as demand changes, so you pay for the December peak only in December. Scalability covers growth; elasticity explicitly includes shrinking back down, which is what kills the idle-fleet waste.

choices: Trade fixed expense for variable expense
Benefit from massive economies of scale
evidence:
CFO: 'Every new project needs a 6-figure server
purchase approved before we write code.'
scenarios.hint: What happens to the capital-approval bottleneck when you pay per hour of usage?
scenarios.prompt: Which cloud benefit directly removes the CFO's 6-figure approval bottleneck?
scenarios.situation: A company's CFO requires capital-expenditure approval before any new project can buy servers, delaying every initiative by months.
scenarios.title: The capex bottleneck
scenarios.why: Trading fixed CapEx for variable OpEx means capacity becomes a pay-as-you-go utility expense, removing the upfront purchase and its approval bottleneck. Economies of scale lower unit cost but don't remove the approval process itself.

evidence:
Requirement: consume managed databases and
analytics with no hardware procurement, pay
per use, deploy in minutes.
scenarios.hint: Which deployment model is defined by services consumed over the internet from a provider?
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment model matches these requirements?
scenarios.situation: A company wants managed databases and analytics with no hardware procurement, pay-per-use pricing, and deployment in minutes.
scenarios.title: No hardware, minutes not months
scenarios.why: A public cloud provides shared, provider-managed infrastructure consumed over the internet with pay-per-use pricing — exactly the described requirements. Private/community/on-premises models keep hardware responsibility with the customer.

choices: Serverless means there are no servers involved at all
Serverless means the provider manages the servers; you manage only code and configuration
Serverless is always cheaper than provisioned capacity
evidence:
Team proposes AWS Lambda for a webhook handler
that runs 200ms, a few times per hour.
Architect flags a misconception in the proposal.
scenarios.hint: Where do the servers go in 'serverless'?
scenarios.prompt: Which statement about serverless is accurate?
scenarios.situation: A team proposes Lambda for a webhook handler that runs a few times per hour. The proposal contains a misconception about serverless.
scenarios.title: Where did the servers go?
scenarios.why: Serverless abstracts server management — the provider runs the servers, scales them, and patches them; you supply code and configuration. Servers still exist. It is not always cheaper (steady high-volume workloads can cost more), and automatic scaling is one of its defining traits.

evidence:
Primary: us-east-1. Requirement: survive the
loss of an entire isolated data-center cluster.
Secondary must be a separate fault domain
within the same geographic area.
scenarios.hint: Regions contain multiple isolated AZs — which term is the isolated data-center cluster itself?
scenarios.prompt: For a secondary fault domain inside the same geographic area, what should the DR plan target?
scenarios.situation: A DR plan requires surviving the loss of an entire isolated data-center cluster, with the secondary site a separate fault domain in the same geographic area.
scenarios.title: Fault domains within a region
scenarios.why: Availability Zones are isolated data-center clusters within a Region, designed as separate fault domains with independent power, cooling, and networking. Multi-AZ deployment is the standard answer to surviving an AZ failure while staying in the same Region.

choices: AWS is responsible for the physical hosts and the hypervisor; the customer is responsible for the guest OS, patching, and data
AWS is responsible for everything up to the application code
The customer is responsible for the physical security of the data center
Responsibility is split 50/50 for every layer
evidence:
Q: You run your app on EC2 instances you manage.
Who patches the guest operating system?
scenarios.hint: On EC2 you control the instance — so which layers move to you?
scenarios.prompt: Who is responsible for what in this EC2 setup?
scenarios.situation: A team runs its application on self-managed EC2 instances and is unsure who patches the guest OS.
scenarios.title: Who patches the guest OS?
scenarios.why: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS handles 'security OF the cloud' (physical facilities, hosts, hypervisor, network infrastructure) while the customer handles 'security IN the cloud' — the guest OS, patching, firewall configuration, and data. On EC2 (IaaS), the guest OS is firmly the customer's job.

evidence:
Auditor asks: who is responsible for the
physical security of AWS data centers and
for the compliance certifications (SOC, ISO)?
scenarios.hint: You will never get a badge to walk into an AWS data center — so who owns that layer?
scenarios.prompt: Who owns physical security and the underlying compliance certifications?
scenarios.situation: An auditor asks who is responsible for physical security of AWS data centers and for maintaining certifications like SOC and ISO.
scenarios.title: Who guards the data center?
scenarios.why: Physical security of data centers and the compliance of the underlying infrastructure are always AWS's responsibility ('security OF the cloud'). Customers inherit these certifications for their own compliance programs but never own the physical layer.

choices: The customer must still classify and protect their data; AWS only protects the underlying service
AWS automatically classifies customer data and applies the right controls
Using RDS transfers data classification responsibility to AWS
Encryption is handled entirely by AWS with no customer involvement
evidence:
Team migrates a customer database to RDS
and assumes AWS now owns data classification
and access decisions.
scenarios.hint: Does moving a database to a managed service change who decides what the data means and who may see it?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the team's assumption?
scenarios.situation: A team migrates its customer database to RDS and assumes AWS now owns data classification and access decisions.
scenarios.title: RDS doesn't read your data policy
scenarios.why: Even with managed services, the customer retains responsibility for their data: classification, access control, and encryption decisions ('security IN the cloud'). AWS secures the RDS platform itself; what the data means and who may see it stays with the customer.

choices: Both: AWS for the platform, the customer for their configurations and data
Neither — compliance is automatic in the cloud
evidence:
Preparing for a PCI DSS assessment of a
workload running on AWS. Who demonstrates
compliance for which parts?
scenarios.hint: Think about who can show evidence for the hypervisor versus who can show evidence for the firewall rules.
scenarios.prompt: How does compliance responsibility divide for the PCI DSS assessment?
scenarios.situation: A company prepares for a PCI DSS assessment of a workload running on AWS.
scenarios.title: Splitting the audit
scenarios.why: Compliance is shared: AWS demonstrates compliance of the underlying platform (customers inherit via AWS Artifact reports), and the customer demonstrates compliance of their configurations, data handling, and access controls. Neither side can do the other's part.

evidence:
Enterprise customer's security team requests
AWS's SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reports before
signing. Where do you get them?
scenarios.hint: Which AWS service is the self-service portal for compliance reports?
scenarios.prompt: Where do you obtain AWS compliance reports?
scenarios.situation: An enterprise customer's security team requests AWS's SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reports during due diligence.
scenarios.title: Show me the SOC 2
scenarios.why: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for downloading AWS compliance and security reports (SOC, ISO, PCI). CloudTrail logs API activity, Config tracks resource configuration, and Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks — none distribute compliance reports.

choices: The customer, through IAM policies and MFA
evidence:
Root account has no MFA. Three admins share
one IAM user with AdministratorAccess.
Who is responsible for fixing this?
scenarios.hint: Access management is the textbook example of 'security IN the cloud' — whose side is it on?
scenarios.prompt: Who is responsible for fixing the access-management gaps?
scenarios.situation: An IAM review finds the root account has no MFA and three admins share one IAM user with AdministratorAccess.
scenarios.title: Shared credentials, shared blame?
scenarios.why: Identity and access management is entirely the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model. AWS provides IAM and MFA as tools, but configuring them correctly — individual users, least privilege, MFA on root — is the customer's job.

choices: AWS Lambda functions behind API Gateway
An EC2 Auto Scaling group with a fixed minimum of 10
An AWS Outposts rack in the office
evidence:
Traffic: 0-500 rps, unpredictable.
Runtime per request: ~300ms.
Team: 2 developers, no ops staff.
scenarios.hint: Which option scales to zero and bills per millisecond?
scenarios.prompt: Which compute option fits best?
scenarios.situation: A marketing site gets unpredictable traffic spikes and the team wants to pay only for the seconds the code runs, with zero server patching.
scenarios.title: Compute for a spiky web tier
scenarios.why: Lambda is serverless: it runs code in response to events, scales automatically from zero, bills per millisecond of execution, and requires no server patching. EC2 options keep idle capacity and ops burden; Outposts is for on-premises needs.

choices: Amazon EBS volumes attached to EC2
evidence:
40 TB video, growing.
Durability target: 99.999999999%.
Access: worldwide via CDN.
scenarios.hint: Which service advertises eleven nines of durability?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage service is the right fit?
scenarios.situation: The team needs to store 40 TB of user-uploaded videos, served worldwide, with 11 nines of durability and no capacity planning.
scenarios.title: Object storage for the media library
scenarios.why: Amazon S3 is object storage designed for exactly this: virtually unlimited scale, 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, and native integration with CloudFront. EBS and instance store are block storage tied to instances; EFS is a file system, not the best fit for global media delivery.

evidence:
Engine: MySQL-compatible.
Ops capacity: zero DBAs.
Needs: automated failover + backups.
scenarios.hint: Which service is 'managed relational database'?
scenarios.prompt: Which database service fits?
scenarios.situation: An app needs a MySQL-compatible relational database, but nobody on the team wants to manage failover, patching, or backups.
scenarios.title: Relational database without the DBA
scenarios.why: Amazon RDS is the managed relational database service: it automates patching, backups, and Multi-AZ failover while offering MySQL-compatible (and other) engines. DynamoDB is NoSQL, Redshift is a data warehouse, and EC2 keeps all the DBA work.

choices: Add read replicas in three more AZs
Put Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) in front of RDS
Move the catalog to Amazon S3
Increase the RDS instance to the largest size
evidence:
RDS CPU: 92% sustained.
Top queries: identical catalog lookups.
Cache hit potential: very high.
scenarios.hint: Which service is purpose-built as an in-memory cache?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most appropriate fix?
scenarios.situation: Read traffic is hammering the RDS primary; 90% of queries repeat the same product catalog lookups. Page latency is climbing.
scenarios.title: Cache in front of the database
scenarios.why: ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching (Redis/Memcached) that absorbs repeated reads, cutting database load and latency. Read replicas help but still hit disk-backed databases per query; S3 is not a low-latency cache; vertical scaling is expensive and doesn't address the repeated-query pattern.

choices: Private subnets + NAT gateway for everything
Private subnets + VPC endpoints (gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB)
A second VPC peered to the first
evidence:
App tier: private subnets only, no public IPs.
Must reach S3 and DynamoDB without
traversing the public internet.
scenarios.hint: Which feature connects a VPC to AWS services privately?
scenarios.prompt: Which combination meets the requirement?
scenarios.situation: The security team requires the application tier to have no public IP addresses, with traffic to AWS services staying off the public internet.
scenarios.title: Private network for the VPC
scenarios.why: VPC endpoints let private-subnet resources reach AWS services without going over the public internet — gateway endpoints cover S3 and DynamoDB at no extra charge. A NAT gateway still sends traffic to the public internet; public subnets violate the no-public-IP rule.

choices: Route 53 for DNS routing + CloudFront as the CDN
A single Application Load Balancer in us-east-1
VPC peering between the three regions
AWS Direct Connect from each office
evidence:
Users: US, EU, Asia.
Failover: automatic on regional failure.
Also needs: static site hosting + CDN.
scenarios.hint: Which two services are AWS's global DNS and CDN?
scenarios.prompt: Which services provide global routing with health-based failover?
scenarios.situation: Users in the US, EU, and Asia need low-latency access to the app, and failover must be automatic if a region has problems.
scenarios.title: DNS and the global front door
scenarios.why: Route 53 provides global DNS-based routing with health checks and failover policies, while CloudFront caches content at edge locations worldwide for low latency. A single ALB is regional; VPC peering connects networks but doesn't route users; Direct Connect is private office connectivity, not user-facing.

choices: Switch to a larger instance to finish queries faster
Stop the instance nights/weekends or move to Aurora Serverless v2
Buy a 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instance
evidence:
RDS db.m5.large On-Demand: $168/mo.
Utilization: 08:00-18:00 weekdays only.
scenarios.hint: If it's idle 128 hours a week, what happens to the cost when it isn't running?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most cost-effective change?
scenarios.situation: A dev database runs 24/7 but is only queried during business hours. The bill shows it as one of the top charges.
scenarios.title: The always-on dev database
scenarios.why: Paying On-Demand for idle hours is pure waste; stopping the instance (or using serverless that scales to near-zero) eliminates the unused cost. Reserved Instances commit you to 24/7 usage you don't have; S3 can't run a relational database.

choices: Compute Savings Plans or Reserved Instances (1- or 3-year)
evidence:
12x EC2 c6i.xlarge, avg CPU 62%, 24/7,
unchanged for 14 months.
scenarios.hint: Which pricing rewards you for committing to steady usage?
scenarios.prompt: Which pricing model minimizes cost?
scenarios.situation: Production web servers run at steady utilization 24/7, and the architecture is stable — no planned changes for the next two years.
scenarios.title: Steady-state production fleet
scenarios.why: Steady, predictable, long-lived usage is the textbook case for commitment discounts: Savings Plans or Reserved Instances cut compute cost significantly versus On-Demand. Spot is for interruptible work; Dedicated Hosts address compliance, not cost.

choices: AWS Cost Explorer with cost allocation tags
evidence:
Line: EC2-Other / NAT Gateway data
processing: $4,120. No project tag.
scenarios.hint: What has to exist on the resources before the bill can be split by team?
scenarios.prompt: Which billing feature answers 'who spent what' first?
scenarios.situation: Finance flags a surprise charge. Nobody can say which team or project caused it.
scenarios.title: Who spent $4,000 on NAT?
scenarios.why: Cost allocation tags let you attribute spend to teams/projects, and Cost Explorer visualizes it. But tags must be applied first — untagged spend is exactly why the invoice is a mystery. Free Tier calculator estimates; Trusted Advisor gives recommendations, not attribution.

choices: Free Tier only covers the first 100 hours
t3.micro is not Free Tier eligible
Free Tier data transfer out is limited (15 GB/month); the excess is billed
The Free Tier expired after 30 days
evidence:
EC2 t3.micro 750h: $0.00 (Free Tier)
Data Transfer Out: 200 GB: $18.00
scenarios.hint: Which line item on the bill is non-zero?
scenarios.prompt: Why was there a charge?
scenarios.situation: A developer stayed 'within Free Tier' but got billed. They ran a t3.micro 750 hours/month and transferred 200 GB out to the internet.
scenarios.title: The Free Tier surprise
scenarios.why: The AWS Free Tier includes 750 hours/month of t2/t3.micro and 15 GB/month of data transfer out for 12 months — usage beyond those allowances is billed at standard rates. The instance hours were free; the 200 GB transfer was not.

choices: AWS Budgets alert + AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
AWS Budgets with an alert and an action (e.g., stop EC2 / restrict IAM) on threshold breach
evidence:
Budget: $200 hard cap.
Need: notify at $160; prevent spend beyond $200.
scenarios.hint: Which service is literally named for tracking spend against a limit?
scenarios.prompt: Which combination provides both?
scenarios.situation: A weekend hackathon team gets a $200 AWS budget. They need an alert at 80% and a hard stop before overspend.
scenarios.title: Budget guardrails for the hackathon
scenarios.why: AWS Budgets tracks spend against a budget, sends alerts at thresholds, and supports budget actions that can restrict resources when a threshold is breached. Anomaly detection finds unusual spend but doesn't enforce caps; CloudWatch alarms monitor metrics, not budgets.

evidence:
Daily backups, ~500 GB/mo growth.
Reads: almost never. Retention: 7 years.
Restore SLA: 12 hours acceptable.
scenarios.hint: Which class trades retrieval speed for the lowest storage price?
scenarios.prompt: Which S3 storage class is the best fit?
scenarios.situation: Backups are written daily, rarely read, must be retained 7 years, and restore can take up to 12 hours.
scenarios.title: S3 storage classes, real workload
scenarios.why: Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 class, designed for long-term retention with retrieval in hours — matching the 7-year, 12-hour-restore profile. Standard and Standard-IA cost far more for rarely-accessed data; Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring fees unsuited to a pure-archive pattern.

choices: Enable MFA on root, then create individual IAM users and stop using root
Just enable MFA on root and keep sharing it
Move the password to a more private channel
evidence:
Daily logins as root (5 people).
MFA: not enabled. Password: in #general.
scenarios.hint: Can the root user be deleted? If not, what's the next best thing?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first remediation?
scenarios.situation: The root user of a new AWS account is used daily by the whole team, with no MFA and a password shared in a chat channel.
scenarios.title: Locking the front door
scenarios.why: Best practice: lock the root user away — enable MFA on it, then create individual IAM users with least-privilege permissions and use root only for tasks that require it. The root user cannot be deleted, and sharing it (even with MFA) destroys accountability.

choices: A policy allowing ec2:RebootInstances on that specific instance only
No permissions; ask an admin each time
scenarios.hint: What's the smallest permission that still lets them do the task?
scenarios.prompt: What should they have instead?
scenarios.situation: A junior developer needs to restart a single EC2 instance for testing. They were given AdministratorAccess 'to keep things simple.'
scenarios.title: Least privilege in practice
scenarios.why: Least privilege means granting only the permissions needed: ec2:RebootInstances scoped to the specific instance ARN. AdministratorAccess for a reboot is excessive; PowerUserAccess is still far too broad; zero permissions blocks legitimate work.

choices: Delete the repo and hope nobody saw it
Deactivate/delete the access key immediately, review CloudTrail, rotate
evidence:
Key AKIA... committed to public repo
at 14:02. Current time: 16:10.
CloudTrail: no unusual calls yet.
scenarios.hint: The key is already public. What makes a public key harmless?
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate correct response?
scenarios.situation: An IAM user's access key was accidentally committed to a public GitHub repo two hours ago.
scenarios.title: The leaked access key
scenarios.why: Treat a public exposure as compromised: deactivate or delete the key immediately, review CloudTrail for misuse, then issue a new key. Bots scan GitHub for keys within minutes — deleting the repo doesn't revoke the key, and passwords don't affect access keys.

choices: S3 now applies default server-side encryption (SSE-S3) to new objects; AWS manages those keys
S3 never encrypts unless you configure it per object
Default encryption requires KMS and customer-managed keys
Encryption at rest is the customer's code responsibility
evidence:
Bucket: default settings.
Question: is SSE-S3 on? Who manages keys?
scenarios.hint: What does S3 do to a new object when you configure nothing?
scenarios.prompt: Which statement is accurate?
scenarios.situation: A team assumes S3 encrypts new objects by default and that they must manage keys themselves for every bucket.
scenarios.title: Encryption at rest, by default?
scenarios.why: S3 applies server-side encryption with S3-managed keys (SSE-S3) by default to all new objects. Customers needing control over keys or audit trails can opt into SSE-KMS (AWS-managed or customer-managed keys) — but the default already encrypts at rest.

choices: AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled on CloudFront, Route 53, and ALB at no extra cost
DDoS protection requires Shield Advanced on every resource
WAF alone mitigates volumetric network floods
Customers must build their own scrubbing centers
evidence:
Attack: 300 Gbps UDP flood against
the CloudFront distribution + ALB.
scenarios.hint: Which protection is on by default and free?
scenarios.prompt: Which is true about AWS DDoS protection?
scenarios.situation: A public-facing web app is hit by a volumetric DDoS attack. The team asks which AWS protections apply automatically.
scenarios.title: DDoS at the edge
scenarios.why: AWS Shield Standard is automatically included at no extra cost and protects CloudFront, Route 53, ALB, and others from common network-layer attacks. Shield Advanced adds enhanced detection, cost protection, and DRT support for a fee; WAF filters application-layer requests, not volumetric floods.

choices: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level
Rely on IAM users having strong passwords
evidence:
s3:GetObject allowed for Principal: '*'
on internal-reports bucket.
scenarios.hint: Which setting overrides any bucket's attempt to go public?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest preventive control?
scenarios.situation: A bucket holding internal reports is accidentally made public. The team wants to prevent this class of mistake account-wide.
scenarios.title: Who can see the S3 bucket?
scenarios.why: S3 Block Public Access (account-level) acts as a guardrail that blocks public ACLs and policies regardless of individual bucket settings — prevention, not detection. Monthly checks are detective; passwords and versioning don't address public exposure.

evidence:
Need: <15 min response for critical.
Also: TAM + proactive guidance.
scenarios.hint: Which plan includes a named TAM?
scenarios.prompt: Which support plan is required?
scenarios.situation: The production site is down. The team needs a 15-minute response from AWS support, plus a dedicated Technical Account Manager for architecture guidance.
scenarios.title: Production is down at 2 AM
scenarios.why: Only Enterprise offers sub-15-minute response for business-critical events plus a Technical Account Manager and proactive guidance. Business tops out at longer response targets without a TAM; Developer/Basic lack urgent response entirely.

evidence:
Workloads: dev/test only.
Support: email, business hours,
<24h response on general guidance.
scenarios.hint: Which paid plan is explicitly scoped to non-production use?
scenarios.prompt: Which is the most cost-effective plan?
scenarios.situation: A small team runs dev/test workloads and wants email support during business hours with a <24-hour response for general questions.
scenarios.title: Dev environment, business hours
scenarios.why: Developer plan provides business-hours email support with <24-hour response on general guidance at the lowest paid tier — matching dev/test needs. Basic has no technical support cases; Business/Enterprise are priced for production.

choices: A Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise support plan
evidence:
Current: 7 core checks visible.
Want: all ~200+ checks incl. cost optimization.
scenarios.hint: Trusted Advisor's full checks are a support-plan benefit — which plans?
scenarios.prompt: What unlocks the full Trusted Advisor check set?
scenarios.situation: An engineer wants automated checks for cost optimization, security gaps, and service limits — and wants the full check set, not just the basics.
scenarios.title: Trusted Advisor at 3 AM
scenarios.why: Basic and Developer plans get only the core Trusted Advisor checks; the full set (cost optimization, security, fault tolerance, performance) requires Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise. Config, Inspector, and CloudTrail are separate services.

choices: Open a Service Quotas request; Enterprise TAM can proactively review
Buy Reserved Instances to raise the quota
evidence:
Need: 2x EC2 quota in eu-west-1
before launch. Want: review of
architecture risks too.
scenarios.hint: Which AWS mechanism exists specifically to request limit increases?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right path?
scenarios.situation: A launch next month will need double the current EC2 On-Demand quota in one region. The team wants AWS to raise it ahead of time with guidance.
scenarios.title: Proactive limit increase
scenarios.why: Service quota increases are requested via Service Quotas; an Enterprise TAM can proactively review limits and architecture ahead of big events (Infrastructure Event Management). Quotas don't auto-increase, Developer plan lacks urgent production support, and RIs don't change quotas.

evidence:
Internal tool needs: open/close cases,
read case history via API.
scenarios.hint: Programmatic case management sits above the Developer tier — which plans include it?
scenarios.prompt: Which plans include AWS Support API access?
scenarios.situation: The ops team wants their internal dashboard to open and track AWS Support cases programmatically.
scenarios.title: Support API for the ticket dashboard
scenarios.why: AWS Support API access (programmatic case management) is available on Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, and Enterprise plans — not on Basic or Developer. This is a common exam discriminator between the lower and upper tiers.

choices: Only the 7 core checks (e.g., MFA on root, unrestricted security groups, service limits)
No Trusted Advisor access at all
Checks run only on request via support case
evidence:
Plan: Basic. Question: Trusted Advisor
coverage for security groups and costs?
scenarios.hint: How many checks come with the free tier of support?
scenarios.prompt: What do Basic (and Developer) plans include?
scenarios.situation: A startup on the Basic plan asks what Trusted Advisor gives them for free.
scenarios.title: The seven core checks
scenarios.why: Basic and Developer include the 7 core Trusted Advisor checks covering security (MFA on root, open security groups), service limits, and basic fault tolerance — but not the cost-optimization checks. Full coverage requires Business or higher.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Aws Clf as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Cloud Concepts Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Cloud Concepts is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Cloud Concepts?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Cloud Concepts issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Cloud Concepts is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct approach is as follows: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Cloud Concepts supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Cloud Concepts failure in Aws Clf.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Cloud Concepts
evidence: All Cloud Concepts components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The Shared Responsibility Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Shared Responsibility is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Shared Responsibility?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Shared Responsibility issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Shared Responsibility is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct approach is as follows: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Shared Responsibility supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Shared Responsibility failure in Aws Clf.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Shared Responsibility
evidence: All Shared Responsibility components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here: Ground Floor

scenarios.title: Navigate the Bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You have 30 days before your assessment. You open the bootcamp and see 15 domains, a terminal, drills, and a mock. You feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first week plan?
choices: Complete Start Here, then work the first three core domains in order — lessons with knowledge checks, then their scenarios, then one lab. Establish the daily loop before widening.
Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the structured loop: Start Here orients you, then sequential domains build the foundation scenarios assume. The mock on day one wastes your only baseline and demoralizes; random study leaves gaps the assessment will find. Drills without understanding produce fast wrong answers.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the scenarios assume you already know.
evidence: 30 days available, ~2 hours per day on weekdays

scenarios.title: When You Get Stuck
scenarios.situation: You have failed the same scenario three times. The explanation makes sense when you read it, but you keep choosing wrong under time pressure.
scenarios.prompt: What should you do?
choices: Drop back to the lesson: re-read the concepts, write out the decision process in your own words, then re-attempt the scenario untimed before going timed again.
Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats repeated failure as a signal: the mental model is broken, not the memory. Rebuilding from the lesson concepts — in your own words — repairs the model. Memorizing the answer passes one scenario and fails the next variation. The assessment tests patterns, not instances.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem memory or the underlying mental model?
objectives: Repair mental models from lesson concepts
evidence: Scenario failed 3x: same wrong choice twice, different wrong choice once

domains.name: Compute Deep Dive

scenarios.title: Who Patches the Server?
scenarios.situation: Your company runs its app on EC2. A critical Linux kernel vulnerability is announced. The CTO asks who is responsible for patching.
scenarios.prompt: Per the shared responsibility model, who patches the EC2 guest OS?
choices: The customer: on EC2, AWS manages the hypervisor and physical infrastructure, but the guest OS, applications, and data are the customer's responsibility.
AWS: they manage everything below the application.
It depends on the EC2 pricing model.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the shared-responsibility line for EC2: AWS = security OF the cloud (facilities, hardware, hypervisor); customer = security IN the cloud, which on EC2 includes the guest OS and up. The managed services (RDS, Lambda) shift more upward to AWS — EC2 shifts the least.
scenarios.hint: What does AWS manage on EC2 versus what do you manage?
objectives: Distinguish OF vs IN the cloud
evidence: Critical kernel CVE; fleet of 40 EC2 instances; no patch process

scenarios.title: The Batch Bargain
scenarios.situation: Your team runs nightly video renders: 6 hours, fault-tolerant, deadline 6 AM, currently on On-Demand at $400/night. Finance wants the bill cut.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best pricing move?
choices: Spot Instances: the workload is interruptible and deadline-flexible — checkpointing handles the 2-minute interruption notice, and discounts up to 90% crush the bill.
scenarios.why: The correct answer matches pricing to workload shape: interruptible + flexible deadline = Spot's ideal profile. Reserved Instances demand steady 24/7 usage; Lambda hits the 15-minute wall on 6-hour renders.
scenarios.hint: Which pricing model rewards interruptibility?
evidence: 6-hour nightly renders, checkpointed, deadline 6 AM, $400/night On-Demand

scenarios.title: The 45-Minute Function
scenarios.situation: A developer proposes a Lambda function that processes uploaded videos, averaging 45 minutes per file, triggered by S3 uploads.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this design?
choices: Lambda is too expensive for video.
Lambda's 15-minute maximum execution kills it: 45-minute videos exceed the hard limit. Use AWS Batch, Fargate, or EC2 for long processing — Lambda fits the short glue tasks around it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer names the hard limit: Lambda caps at 15 minutes per invocation, so a 45-minute job cannot complete. The exam tests this boundary constantly — duration is the first Lambda suitability check.
scenarios.hint: What is Lambda's maximum execution time?
evidence: S3 trigger -> Lambda, 45-min average processing per video

scenarios.title: Ship It by Friday
scenarios.situation: A two-person startup must deploy a Node.js app by Friday. No ops experience, no time to configure load balancers or auto-scaling.
scenarios.prompt: Which service fits best?
choices: Elastic Beanstalk: upload the code and AWS provisions the EC2 fleet, load balancer, and scaling — the PaaS option for 'just run my code.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the highest-abstraction fit: Beanstalk exists for exactly this — code in, running app out, with the underlying infrastructure still accessible later. EKS and manual EC2 demand the ops skills the team lacks.
scenarios.hint: Which service minimizes operational burden for code deployment?
evidence: 2-person team, Node.js app, Friday deadline, zero ops experience

scenarios.title: The K8s Question
scenarios.situation: Your team runs microservices on Kubernetes on-premises and wants the same APIs in AWS without managing the control plane. Some workloads are spiky.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best fit?
choices: EKS with Fargate: managed Kubernetes control plane (AWS handles masters) plus serverless workers for the spiky workloads — same K8s APIs, minimal node management.
scenarios.why: The correct answer preserves the team's K8s investment (EKS = managed Kubernetes) while Fargate removes worker-node management for spiky traffic. ECS would force re-platforming off Kubernetes APIs.
scenarios.hint: Which option keeps Kubernetes APIs with managed infrastructure?
evidence: K8s expertise on-prem; spiky microservice traffic; no desire to manage masters

scenarios.title: The Single-AZ Outage
scenarios.situation: A company's entire web tier runs on EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. An AZ power event takes the site down for 4 hours.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture prevents recurrence?
choices: Multi-AZ deployment: instances across at least two AZs behind an Elastic Load Balancer — AZs are isolated failure domains, and the region survives one AZ's failure.
Bigger instances in the same AZ.
scenarios.why: The correct answer uses AZs as designed: each AZ is an isolated data-center cluster, and distributing across them with a load balancer survives single-AZ events. A second region is overkill for an AZ-level failure.
scenarios.hint: What is an Availability Zone's failure-isolation purpose?
evidence: 4-hour outage; all instances in us-east-1a; post-mortem required

scenarios.title: The Steady Bill
scenarios.situation: A company runs 100 EC2 instances 24/7 for its core platform — flat usage for 18 months. They pay full On-Demand rates.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cost-optimization move?
choices: Savings Plans (or Reserved Instances): steady 24/7 usage is the textbook commitment case — up to 72% off for a 1- or 3-year commitment, with Savings Plans offering flexibility across instance families.
scenarios.why: The correct answer commits where usage is predictable: 18 months of flat 24/7 demand will not surprise you, so the commitment discount is nearly free money. Spot risks interruption on the core platform; night shutdowns contradict 24/7.
scenarios.hint: When do commitment discounts pay off?
objectives: Apply Savings Plans to steady workloads
Avoid Spot for core steady state
evidence: 100 instances, 24/7, flat 18 months, full On-Demand pricing

scenarios.title: The Predictable Blog
scenarios.situation: A freelancer needs to host 5 small WordPress sites. Budget is fixed, traffic is low, and AWS's full console feels overwhelming.
scenarios.prompt: What fits best?
choices: Lightsail: flat-rate VPS bundles with predictable monthly pricing and a simplified console — designed for exactly this scale.
scenarios.why: The correct answer matches scale to service: Lightsail's fixed-price simplicity beats EC2's power (and complexity) for five low-traffic sites. Enterprise services would be expensive overkill.
scenarios.hint: Which service targets simple, fixed-price, small-scale hosting?
evidence: 5 WordPress sites, fixed budget, low traffic, minimal AWS experience

domains.name: Database Services

scenarios.title: Standby or Scale?
scenarios.situation: An e-commerce RDS MySQL primary handles checkout writes fine, but product-page reads saturate it every afternoon. The team proposes enabling Multi-AZ.
scenarios.prompt: Will Multi-AZ solve the read saturation?
choices: No: Multi-AZ provides a non-readable standby for failover (availability), not read scaling. Add Read Replicas to absorb the read traffic — or both, for availability AND scale.
scenarios.why: The correct answer keeps the two features straight: Multi-AZ = standby for failover (you cannot query it); Read Replicas = async readable copies for scaling. The exam tests this distinction relentlessly.
scenarios.hint: Can you run queries against a Multi-AZ standby?
evidence: RDS primary CPU 95% on reads, 14:00-17:00 daily; writes fine

scenarios.title: The Global Read Problem
scenarios.situation: A SaaS runs PostgreSQL-compatible RDS in us-east-1. EU users complain about slow dashboards. The team needs fast regional reads with minimal lag.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best move?
choices: Aurora Global Database: PostgreSQL-compatible with cross-region read replicas at under a second of lag — built for exactly this global-read pattern.
Add RDS Read Replicas in eu-west-1.
scenarios.why: The correct answer uses Aurora's global design: sub-second cross-region replication beats RDS cross-region read replicas (higher lag), while keeping PostgreSQL compatibility. DynamoDB would force a rewrite; caching alone does not fix the source.
scenarios.hint: Which service offers sub-second global replication for relational data?
evidence: EU dashboard p95 latency 2.8s; US p95 300ms; Postgres required

scenarios.title: The Session Store
scenarios.situation: A mobile game needs session storage: 200k writes/sec at peak, single-digit millisecond latency, traffic triples on launch weekends.
scenarios.prompt: Which database fits?
choices: DynamoDB On-Demand: serverless key-value at any scale, millisecond latency, and pay-per-request pricing that absorbs the 3x launch spikes without provisioning.
scenarios.why: The correct answer matches the workload adjectives to the service: massive key-value throughput + spiky + millisecond = DynamoDB On-Demand. RDS cannot scale writes this way; Redshift is analytics; Neptune is graphs.
scenarios.hint: Which database scales writes serverlessly with millisecond latency?

scenarios.title: The Analytics Ask
scenarios.situation: Finance runs complex queries over 5 years of sales data (40 TB) every morning. They tried the production RDS and nearly took down checkout.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right architecture?
choices: Redshift: move analytics to a petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse — OLAP belongs off the transactional database, loaded nightly via ETL.
scenarios.why: The correct answer separates OLTP from OLAP: Redshift's columnar, massively-parallel design exists for exactly these scan-heavy queries, and isolating them protects checkout. Bigger RDS just delays the next incident.
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes OLAP from OLTP workloads?
evidence: Morning finance queries saturated RDS; checkout latency spiked 10x

scenarios.title: The Hot Key
scenarios.situation: Product pages hit the database for the same top-100 items thousands of times per second. RDS CPU is pegged; the data changes hourly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective fix?
choices: ElastiCache (Redis) in front of RDS: cache the hot items with a 1-hour TTL — microsecond reads absorb the repeated traffic and RDS breathes again.
scenarios.why: The correct answer caches the repeatable reads: identical queries thousands of times per second with hourly changes are the textbook cache case. Replicas and bigger instances scale expensively what caching solves cheaply.
scenarios.hint: When does caching beat scaling the database?
evidence: Top-100 items, 3k reads/sec, data changes hourly, RDS CPU 98%

scenarios.title: The Fraud Graph
scenarios.situation: A bank needs to find fraud rings: accounts connected through shared devices, addresses, and phone numbers, several hops deep. SQL self-joins are timing out.
scenarios.prompt: Which database fits?
choices: Neptune: a managed graph database built for multi-hop relationship queries — traversals that choke relational joins run natively on graph structure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer matches 'relationship-heavy, multi-hop' to the graph service. Relational joins explode combinatorially on deep traversals; Neptune's graph engine is purpose-built for exactly this.
scenarios.hint: Which workload adjective points to a graph database?
evidence: 'Accounts within 4 hops of flagged device' — SQL times out at 120s

scenarios.title: The Zero-Downtime Move
scenarios.situation: A hospital must migrate its Oracle patient database to AWS with near-zero downtime — the system cannot go offline during business hours.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach fits?
choices: DMS with ongoing replication: full load plus continuous change-data capture keeps AWS in sync, then cut over in a brief window — SCT converts the Oracle schema to the target engine.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the minimal-downtime pattern: DMS replicates continuously so the cutover window shrinks to minutes, and SCT handles Oracle-to-target conversion. Dump/restore means hours of downtime.
scenarios.hint: Which service replicates a database continuously during migration?
evidence: Patient system, zero business-hours downtime, Oracle source

scenarios.title: The MongoDB Move
scenarios.situation: A startup's app is built on MongoDB. They want a managed AWS database without rewriting their queries and drivers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best fit?
choices: DocumentDB: MongoDB-compatible managed document database — existing drivers and queries largely work against the AWS-managed endpoint.
scenarios.why: The correct answer preserves the existing investment: DocumentDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol, so migration avoids the rewrite that DynamoDB's different API would demand.
scenarios.hint: Which service offers MongoDB compatibility on AWS?
evidence: 200k lines on MongoDB drivers; team wants managed AWS

scenarios.situation: You are about to start the Cloud Architecture Project capstone. You have limited lab time and want maximum interview value.

Start building immediately — planning wastes lab time.
Attempt the most impressive architecture possible to stand out.
Build whatever is easiest to finish quickly.

domains.name: Analytics Services Overview

scenarios.title: The Log Query Bill
scenarios.situation: Your team queries 2 TB of ALB logs in S3 with Athena daily. The bill is $300/month and growing. The logs are raw CSV, unpartitioned.
scenarios.prompt: What cuts the Athena cost most?
choices: Convert to Parquet, partition by date, and compress: columnar format + partition pruning slashes data scanned per query — the dominant cost lever since Athena bills per TB scanned.
scenarios.why: The correct answer attacks the pricing model: Athena charges per TB scanned, so Parquet (columnar, compressed) plus date partitioning (prune irrelevant data) multiplies down every query's cost. Querying less treats the symptom.
scenarios.hint: How does Athena pricing make format and partitioning a cost decision?
objectives: Optimize Athena with Parquet and partitioning
evidence: 2 TB raw CSV scanned daily; $300/mo and growing

scenarios.title: The Nightly Spark Job
scenarios.situation: A data team runs a 90-minute Spark job nightly on 1.5 TB. They keep an EMR cluster running 24/7 'so it is ready.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the cost fix?
choices: Transient EMR clusters: spin up for the 90-minute job, terminate after — 22.5 idle hours a day of cluster cost vanishes; EMR's managed setup makes spin-up cheap.
scenarios.why: The correct answer kills the idle time: a nightly 90-minute job needs ~2 hours of cluster, not 24. Transient clusters are EMR's core cost pattern; Lambda cannot run 90-minute Spark.
scenarios.hint: What is EMR's cost-optimal pattern for scheduled batch?

scenarios.title: The Schema Drift
scenarios.situation: Marketing uploads CSVs with changing columns weekly. Analysts hand-edit table definitions each time before Athena queries work.
scenarios.prompt: What automates this?
choices: A Glue crawler: it scans the S3 data, infers schema changes, and updates the Data Catalog — Athena queries keep working without hand-edited DDL.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is Glue's signature feature: crawlers auto-discover and evolve schema in the shared Catalog. Hand-maintaining DDL against weekly drift is toil the crawler eliminates.
scenarios.hint: Which Glue feature handles evolving schemas automatically?
objectives: Use Glue crawlers for schema discovery
evidence: Weekly column changes; analysts hand-edit DDL; queries break regularly

scenarios.title: The Clickstream Loader
scenarios.situation: Product wants clickstream events in the S3 data lake within minutes, queryable by Athena. No custom per-event logic needed; the team is small.
scenarios.prompt: Which ingestion service fits?
choices: Kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers.
Amazon Data Firehose: managed streaming delivery to S3 with batching, compression, and Parquet conversion — no consumer code or shard management for the small team.
scenarios.why: The correct answer picks managed over flexible: with no custom processing and a small team, Firehose's zero-admin delivery beats Data Streams' consumer/shard management. EMR and DMS are wrong stages entirely.
scenarios.hint: When does Firehose beat Data Streams?
objectives: Land streams in S3 for Athena
evidence: Clickstream -> S3 in minutes; no custom logic; 3-person team

scenarios.title: The Dashboard Ask
scenarios.situation: Executives want daily sales dashboards. No BI infrastructure exists, usage is 20 viewers, and IT will not manage servers.
scenarios.prompt: What fits?
choices: QuickSight: serverless BI with pay-per-session pricing — dashboards over Athena/RDS/Redshift with zero servers for IT to run.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the serverless BI service: QuickSight's per-session pricing fits 20 viewers and its managed nature fits the no-servers constraint. Self-hosted EC2 contradicts the requirement.
scenarios.hint: Which service provides dashboards without server management?
evidence: 20 viewers, daily dashboards, zero server management

scenarios.title: Name That Stage
scenarios.situation: A question describes: 'IoT temperature data must be collected continuously, stored durably, transformed nightly, and shown on dashboards.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the exam technique for mapping services?
choices: Pipeline thinking: assign each verb a stage — collect (Kinesis), store (S3), transform (Glue/EMR), visualize (QuickSight) — then pick the service per stage instead of guessing one service for everything.
Pick the most powerful service mentioned.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the method, not a service: decomposing the scenario into pipeline stages turns 'which service' into five easy lookups. CLF-C02 analytics questions are stage questions wearing service costumes.
scenarios.hint: How do you decompose a multi-requirement analytics scenario?
evidence: collected continuously / stored durably / transformed nightly / dashboards

scenarios.title: Spectrum vs Redshift
scenarios.situation: An analyst needs to join 50 GB of hot sales data with 10 TB of cold historical data in S3, queried weekly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most cost-effective approach?
choices: Redshift Spectrum: query the cold S3 data in place from Redshift without loading it — hot data stays in the cluster, cold data stays cheap in S3, joined in one query.
scenarios.why: The correct answer keeps cold data cold: Spectrum extends Redshift queries to S3, so the 10 TB avoids expensive cluster storage while still joining with hot data. Loading it all wastes money; Athena alone cannot join efficiently at this shape.
scenarios.hint: How do you query S3 data from Redshift without loading it?
objectives: Use Redshift Spectrum for S3 joins
evidence: 50 GB hot + 10 TB cold in S3; weekly join queries

scenarios.title: Real-Time Fraud
scenarios.situation: A payment company must score transactions for fraud within 2 seconds, with custom ML per transaction, at 10k TPS.
scenarios.prompt: Which streaming design fits?
choices: Kinesis Data Streams with consumer applications: ordered per-key processing, custom ML scoring logic per event, and shard-scaled throughput for 10k TPS — Firehose cannot run custom per-record logic.
scenarios.why: The correct answer needs custom per-event processing at scale: Data Streams gives consumers full control with ordering guarantees per shard key. Firehose is delivery-only; batch options miss the 2-second SLA.
scenarios.hint: Which service supports custom per-record stream processing?
objectives: Choose Data Streams for custom logic
evidence: Fraud score in <2s per transaction; 10k TPS; custom ML per event

domains.name: Migration to AWS

scenarios.title: Pick the R
scenarios.situation: A retailer must vacate its data center in 5 months: 400 VMs, no code changes allowed by the business, optimization 'later.'
scenarios.prompt: Which strategy fits?
choices: Rehost: lift-and-shift the VMs as-is (via MGN) to meet the hard deadline with zero application changes — optimization becomes the explicit phase 2.
scenarios.why: The correct answer honors the constraints: 5 months + no code changes rules out Refactor and Repurchase. Rehost meets the deadline; the 'later' optimization must be a scheduled phase, not a wish.
scenarios.hint: Which R means move as-is with no changes?
evidence: 5-month exit, 400 VMs, zero code changes permitted

scenarios.title: The Tired DBA
scenarios.situation: A company migrates its self-managed PostgreSQL to AWS. The DBA team spends 30% of its time patching and managing replicas, and wants out of that work.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach fits?
choices: Replatform to RDS/Aurora PostgreSQL: move with a small change (managed database instead of self-managed) that eliminates the patching/replica toil while keeping Postgres compatibility.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the 'lift and reshape' middle: changing the platform (self-managed → managed) during migration captures the operational win without a rewrite. Rehost preserves the toil; DynamoDB forces a data-model rewrite.
scenarios.hint: Which R changes the platform slightly for managed benefits?
evidence: DBAs spend 30% time on patching/replicas; Postgres must stay

scenarios.title: The Stalled Migration
scenarios.situation: Six months into a migration, teams spin up resources with no tagging, nobody knows the cloud bill owners, and security has not reviewed a single workload.
scenarios.prompt: Which CAF perspectives failed?
choices: Business — migrations never need business cases.
Governance (cost controls, tagging, account structure) and Security (controls traveling with workloads) — the migration moved servers while the guardrails stayed behind.
scenarios.why: The correct answer names the non-technical gap: untagged spend with no owners is Governance; unreviewed workloads are Security. CAF exists because migrations fail on exactly these perspectives while the technology works fine.
scenarios.hint: Which perspectives cover cost control and compliance?
evidence: No tagging, unknown bill owners, zero security reviews at month 6

scenarios.title: Servers vs Databases
scenarios.situation: A factory migrates 150 VMs and 3 SQL Server databases to AWS with minimal downtime. The architect proposes DMS for everything.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the plan?
choices: Wrong tool for servers: DMS migrates DATABASES; the 150 VMs need Application Migration Service (MGN). Use MGN for servers, DMS (+SCT) for the SQL Server databases.
scenarios.why: The correct answer keeps the tool boundary crisp: MGN = server lift-and-shift with continuous replication; DMS = database migration. The exam plants exactly this confusion as a distractor.
scenarios.hint: Which service lift-and-shifts servers, and which migrates databases?
evidence: 150 VMs + 3 SQL Server DBs; architect proposed DMS for all

scenarios.title: The Bandwidth Wall
scenarios.situation: A media company must move 3 PB of archives to S3. Their uplink is 500 Mbps and the CFO will not pay for a bigger circuit.
scenarios.prompt: What is the practical path?
choices: Snowball fleet (or Snowmobile assessment): 3 PB over 500 Mbps takes ~1.5 years — physical transfer devices are the only sane option at this scale and bandwidth.
S3 multipart upload from the office.
scenarios.why: The correct answer does the transfer math: petabytes over megabits means years — Snow devices convert network-years into shipping-days. The CFO's constraint actually forces the Snow decision.
scenarios.hint: At what scale does physical transfer beat the network?
objectives: Apply Snow family at petabyte scale
evidence: 3 PB / 500 Mbps ≈ 550 days; CFO rejects circuit upgrade

scenarios.title: The File Share
scenarios.situation: A design studio needs its 30 TB NFS file share in S3, synced nightly, with validation that files arrived intact.
scenarios.prompt: Which service fits?
choices: DataSync: managed, fast NFS/SMB-to-S3 transfer with scheduling, bandwidth throttling, and built-in data validation — purpose-built for this.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the file-transfer service: DataSync handles protocols, scheduling, and integrity checking natively. Snowcone is for edge/offline; DMS is databases; rsync is toil.
scenarios.hint: Which service moves file shares to S3 with validation?
evidence: 30 TB NFS -> S3, nightly sync, integrity validation

scenarios.title: Wave Zero
scenarios.situation: An enterprise plans to migrate 300 applications. The proposal starts with 'migrate the ERP in month one to show progress.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the sequencing?
choices: Skip the landing zone to save time.

Wave discipline: start with the landing zone + a low-risk pilot (Wave 0), then independent apps — the coupled ERP core migrates LAST, after the pattern is proven. Leading with the hardest workload maximizes blast radius.
scenarios.why: The correct answer sequences by risk and dependency: Wave 0 proves the landing zone and runbooks on something forgiving; the ERP's coupling makes it the worst possible first move. Progress theater is not progress.
scenarios.hint: How should migration waves be sequenced?
evidence: 300 apps; ERP (most coupled) proposed for month one

scenarios.title: The Unknown Estate
scenarios.situation: A company acquired a data center with 600 undocumented servers. Nobody knows what depends on what, or what anything costs to run.
scenarios.prompt: What comes before wave planning?
choices: Discovery and assessment: Application Discovery Service / Migration Evaluator to map dependencies and build the TCO business case — you cannot sequence what you cannot see.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is assess-before-migrate: dependency mapping prevents wave collisions and the TCO model justifies the program. Migrating blind turns unknown coupling into outages.
scenarios.hint: What must precede migration wave planning?
evidence: 600 undocumented servers; zero dependency knowledge; no cost baseline

domains.name: Well-Architected Framework

scenarios.title: Name the Pillar
scenarios.situation: A team enables MFA everywhere, encrypts all EBS volumes with KMS, and turns on CloudTrail with immutable log storage.
scenarios.prompt: Which pillar do these practices belong to?
choices: Security: identity controls (MFA), encryption (KMS), and traceability (CloudTrail) are the Security pillar's core practices.
scenarios.why: The correct answer maps practices to pillars: MFA + encryption + audit logging is the Security pillar's unmistakable signature. The exam's pillar questions are practice-recognition, not definition recall.
scenarios.hint: Which practices are the Security pillar's signature?
evidence: MFA enforced, KMS encryption, immutable CloudTrail logs

scenarios.title: The 3 AM Test
scenarios.situation: A database fails over manually: an operator gets paged, runs the runbook, and restores service in 40 minutes. Twice this quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What does the Reliability pillar prescribe?
choices: Automated recovery: Multi-AZ with automatic failover removes the operator from the critical path — the pillar demands recovery WITHOUT human intervention, tested regularly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the pillar's core principle: design systems that recover automatically. Manual runbooks, however fast, violate 'automatic recovery from failure' — and 40 minutes of downtime twice a quarter is the cost.
scenarios.hint: What does 'automatic recovery from failure' require?
evidence: 2 manual failovers this quarter, 40 min MTTR each

scenarios.title: The Idle Fleet
scenarios.situation: Cost Explorer shows 30 EC2 instances averaging 4% CPU for 6 months, plus 2 TB of unattached EBS volumes. Nobody claims them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the Cost Optimization response?
choices: Hygiene first: terminate or right-size the idle instances, delete unattached volumes (snapshot first), tag everything with owners, and set up Trusted Advisor + Budgets alerts so waste cannot accumulate silently again.
scenarios.why: The correct answer treats waste as the default state: the pillar's first move is eliminating what should not exist, then committing only on the right-sized remainder. Reserving waste just discounts it.
scenarios.hint: What is the first step of cost optimization?
evidence: 30 instances at 4% CPU, 2 TB unattached EBS, 6 months

scenarios.title: The Tradeoff Question
scenarios.situation: A proposal cuts cost 30% by running production in a single AZ. The architect objects on Reliability grounds.
scenarios.prompt: How does the Framework resolve this?
choices: Requirements bound optimization: the Framework demands BOTH pillars be satisfied — cost cannot be cut below the reliability the business requires. Single-AZ for production fails Reliability regardless of savings; find cost wins that preserve the SLA.
scenarios.why: The correct answer applies the Framework as a system: pillars constrain each other, and business requirements set the floor. 'Cheapest' is never correct when it violates a stated reliability requirement.
scenarios.hint: How do pillars interact under competing proposals?
evidence: -30% cost via single-AZ production; SLA requires 99.9%

scenarios.title: The Green Question
scenarios.situation: A company wants to reduce its cloud carbon footprint. Its workloads run on older instance types at 15% average utilization.
scenarios.prompt: What helps most?
choices: Raise utilization with modern efficient instances: migrate to Graviton (better price-performance per watt), enable auto-scaling to kill idle capacity, and prefer serverless/managed services — efficiency is the sustainability lever.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is the Sustainability pillar's core mechanic: higher utilization + efficient silicon = less energy per unit of work. Offsets do not change the footprint; the other options are irrelevant or harmful.
scenarios.hint: What is the Sustainability pillar's primary lever?

scenarios.title: The Change Failure
scenarios.situation: Production changes are big-bang Friday deploys. Rollbacks take hours, and every deploy is feared.
scenarios.prompt: Which pillar's practices fix this?
choices: Operational Excellence: small reversible changes, IaC, automated testing, and deployment safeguards (canary/blue-green) — the pillar's 'evolve safely' principle replaces fear with routine.
scenarios.why: The correct answer maps the practice set: IaC, small reversible changes, and safe deployment patterns are Operational Excellence signatures. The fear is the symptom; the change process is the disease.
scenarios.hint: Which practices define Operational Excellence?
evidence: Big-bang Friday deploys, hours-long rollbacks, deploy fear

scenarios.title: The Review Cadence
scenarios.situation: A team did one Well-Architected review at launch two years ago. The architecture has tripled in size since.
scenarios.prompt: What does the Framework recommend?
choices: Review as a habit: re-run the Well-Architected review on significant changes and on a cadence — architectures drift, new services appear, and the review catches drift before incidents do.
scenarios.why: The correct answer treats the review as continuous improvement, not a checkbox: the Framework is a living practice, and a two-year-old review describes an architecture that no longer exists.
scenarios.hint: How often should architectures be reviewed?
objectives: Treat the Framework as living practice
evidence: One review 2 years ago; architecture 3x larger since

lessons.title: Cloud Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: Cloud value proposition: the cloud's core value proposition is eliminating undifferentiated heavy lifting — racking, powering, cooling, and repairing physical infrastructure — so teams spend their time on the product.
Elasticity vs scalability: scalability covers growth; elasticity explicitly includes shrinking back down, which is what kills the idle-fleet waste.
CapEx to OpEx: trading fixed CapEx for variable OpEx means capacity becomes a pay-as-you-go utility expense, removing the upfront purchase and its approval bottleneck.
Apply the shared responsibility model to every architecture decision: know exactly which security tasks are yours versus AWS's for each service you use.

example.code:
CFO: 'Every new project needs a 6-figure server
purchase approved before we write code.'
example.walkthrough: Trading fixed CapEx for variable OpEx means capacity becomes a pay-as-you-go utility expense, removing the upfront purchase and its approval bottleneck. Economies of scale lower unit cost but don't remove the approval process itself.

pitfalls: Common trap: serverless applications cannot scale automatically.
Common trap: serverless means there are no servers involved at all.
Common trap: serverless is always cheaper than provisioned capacity.
Common trap: it means servers are located in a single data center for lower latency.

lessons.title: Shared Responsibility — Core concepts
concepts: Shared responsibility model: under the shared responsibility model, AWS handles 'security OF the cloud' (physical facilities, hosts, hypervisor, network infrastructure) while the customer handles 'security IN the cloud' — the guest OS, patching, firewall configuration, and data.
IaaS responsibilities: on EC2 (IaaS), the guest OS is firmly the customer's job.

Security OF the cloud: physical security of data centers and the compliance of the underlying infrastructure are always AWS's responsibility ('security OF the cloud'). Even with managed services, the customer retains responsibility for their data: classification, access control, and encryption decisions ('security IN the cloud').
Security IN the cloud: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for downloading AWS compliance and security reports (SOC, ISO, PCI).

Compliance is shared: AWS demonstrates compliance of the underlying platform (customers inherit via AWS Artifact reports), and the customer demonstrates compliance of their configurations, data handling, and access controls.

example.code:
Q: You run your app on EC2 instances you manage.
Who patches the guest operating system?
example.walkthrough: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS handles 'security OF the cloud' (physical facilities, hosts, hypervisor, network infrastructure) while the customer handles 'security IN the cloud' — the guest OS, patching, firewall configuration, and data. On EC2 (IaaS), the guest OS is firmly the customer's job.

pitfalls: Common trap: the customer must still classify and protect their data; AWS only protects the underlying service.
Common trap: using RDS transfers data classification responsibility to AWS.
Common trap: the customer is responsible for the physical security of the data center.
Common trap: encryption is handled entirely by AWS with no customer involvement.

lessons.title: Core Services — Core concepts
concepts: Compute services: VPC endpoints let private-subnet resources reach AWS services without going over the public internet — gateway endpoints cover S3 and DynamoDB at no extra charge.
Serverless: lambda is serverless: it runs code in response to events, scales automatically from zero, bills per millisecond of execution, and requires no server patching.
Storage services: amazon S3 is object storage designed for exactly this: virtually unlimited scale, 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, and native integration with CloudFront.
S3: read replicas help but still hit disk-backed databases per query; S3 is not a low-latency cache; vertical scaling is expensive and doesn't address the repeated-query pattern.

Database services: elastiCache provides managed in-memory caching (Redis/Memcached) that absorbs repeated reads, cutting database load and latency. Amazon RDS is the managed relational database service: it automates patching, backups, and Multi-AZ failover while offering MySQL-compatible (and other) engines.

example.code:
RDS CPU: 92% sustained.
Top queries: identical catalog lookups.
Cache hit potential: very high.
example.walkthrough: ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching (Redis/Memcached) that absorbs repeated reads, cutting database load and latency. Read replicas help but still hit disk-backed databases per query; S3 is not a low-latency cache; vertical scaling is expensive and doesn't address the repeated-query pattern.

pitfalls: Common trap: increase the RDS instance to the largest size.
Common trap: a second VPC peered to the first.
Common trap: VPC peering between the three regions.
Common trap: an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a fixed minimum of 10.

lessons.title: Pricing & Billing — Core concepts
concepts: Cost allocation tags let you attribute spend to teams/projects, and Cost Explorer visualizes it. Steady, predictable, long-lived usage is the textbook case for commitment discounts: Savings Plans or Reserved Instances cut compute cost significantly versus On-Demand.
On-Demand vs serverless: paying On-Demand for idle hours is pure waste; stopping the instance (or using serverless that scales to near-zero) eliminates the unused cost.

Cost allocation tags: but tags must be applied first — untagged spend is exactly why the invoice is a mystery. Standard and Standard-IA cost far more for rarely-accessed data; Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring fees unsuited to a pure-archive pattern.
Use the AWS Pricing Calculator before deploying: model the workload, compare pricing options (On-Demand vs Reserved vs Spot), and set up billing alerts on day one.

example.code:
EC2 t3.micro 750h: $0.00 (Free Tier)
Data Transfer Out: 200 GB: $18.00
example.walkthrough: The AWS Free Tier includes 750 hours/month of t2/t3.micro and 15 GB/month of data transfer out for 12 months — usage beyond those allowances is billed at standard rates. The instance hours were free; the 200 GB transfer was not.

pitfalls: Common trap: AWS Budgets alert + AWS Cost Anomaly Detection.
Common trap: the AWS Free Tier calculator.
Common trap: free Tier only covers the first 100 hours.
Common trap: t3.micro is not Free Tier eligible.

lessons.title: Security Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Root user security: best practice: lock the root user away — enable MFA on it, then create individual IAM users with least-privilege permissions and use root only for tasks that require it.
Least privilege means granting only the permissions needed: ec2:RebootInstances scoped to the specific instance ARN.
IAM policies: S3 Block Public Access (account-level) acts as a guardrail that blocks public ACLs and policies regardless of individual bucket settings — prevention, not detection.
Enable MFA on the root account and all IAM users on day one: it is the single highest-leverage security action in any AWS account.

example.code:
{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"*",
"Resource":"*"} // attached to dev
example.walkthrough: Least privilege means granting only the permissions needed: ec2:RebootInstances scoped to the specific instance ARN. AdministratorAccess for a reboot is excessive; PowerUserAccess is still far too broad; zero permissions blocks legitimate work.

pitfalls: Common trap: dDoS protection requires Shield Advanced on every resource.
Common trap: encryption at rest is the customer's code responsibility.
Common trap: change the IAM user's password.
Common trap: default encryption requires KMS and customer-managed keys.

lessons.title: Support Plans — Core concepts
concepts: Support plans: AWS Support API access (programmatic case management) is available on Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, and Enterprise plans — not on Basic or Developer.

Enterprise: service quota increases are requested via Service Quotas; an Enterprise TAM can proactively review limits and architecture ahead of big events (Infrastructure Event Management). Only Enterprise offers sub-15-minute response for business-critical events plus a Technical Account Manager and proactive guidance.

Developer: basic and Developer include the 7 core Trusted Advisor checks covering security (MFA on root, open security groups), service limits, and basic fault tolerance — but not the cost-optimization checks.
Support plan benefits: developer plan provides business-hours email support with <24-hour response on general guidance at the lowest paid tier — matching dev/test needs.

example.code:
Plan: Basic. Question: Trusted Advisor
coverage for security groups and costs?
example.walkthrough: Basic and Developer include the 7 core Trusted Advisor checks covering security (MFA on root, open security groups), service limits, and basic fault tolerance — but not the cost-optimization checks. Full coverage requires Business or higher.

pitfalls: Common trap: checks run only on request via support case.
Common trap: quotas increase automatically with usage.
Common trap: all checks including cost optimization.
Common trap: buy Reserved Instances to raise the quota.

lessons.title: AWS Cloud Practitioner Essentials — Core concepts
concepts: AWS's global infrastructure is Regions (geographic areas), Availability Zones (isolated data centers inside a Region), and edge locations (CloudFront/Route 53 points of presence). Design across AZs for resilience; pick Regions for latency, compliance, and price.

The shared responsibility model splits security: AWS secures the infrastructure OF the cloud, you secure what you put IN it. The line moves with abstraction — EC2 leaves the OS to you, RDS and Lambda take more back.
The core service families are compute (EC2, Lambda), storage (S3, EBS, EFS), databases (RDS, DynamoDB), and networking (VPC). Match the service to the access pattern, not the brand name.

Pricing models are On-Demand (flexible), Savings Plans/Reserved Instances (commitment discounts for steady use), and Spot (deep discounts for interruptible work). Cost control is mostly about turning things off and rightsizing, not hunting discounts first.
Identity is the perimeter: IAM users, groups, roles, and policies control who can do what. Least privilege from day one prevents the breach you never hear about.

example.code:
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[*].ZoneName' --output text
example.walkthrough: This lists the AZs in a Region so you can see the fault-isolation units your architecture should span. Run it for a few Regions to build the habit of thinking multi-AZ from the start.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating a Region and an AZ as the same thing — resilience comes from AZs, latency/compliance from Regions.
Common trap: putting production databases on Spot or single-AZ EC2 to save money, then paying for it in downtime.
Common trap: assuming S3 needs 'replication across AZs' — S3 already stores data redundantly across AZs in a Region.
Common trap: forgetting that with managed services the responsibility line moves — RDS patches the OS, but you still own the data and access control.
