lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Aws Clf move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it top to bottom: each domain builds on the previous one, and later scenarios assume earlier knowledge
Every lesson ends with a knowledge check: answer correctly and the lesson auto-completes. Wrong answers send you back to review — this is verification, not clicking through
Scenarios are timed decision exercises with evidence to examine. Treat each like the real thing: read everything, decide, then commit
Your progress saves automatically. Domains unlock as you complete prerequisites — the path guides you, but you set the pace

example.code:
LEARN path: lessons -> scenarios -> labs -> drills
TERMINAL: hands-on command practice
MOCK: full timed assessment when ready

Suggested daily loop:
  1. Complete 2-3 lessons (with knowledge checks)
  2. Work 3-5 scenarios in those domains
  3. Run 1 lab end-to-end
  4. 10 minutes of drills
example.walkthrough: The bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually work: learn the concept, apply it under realistic conditions, then prove it in the lab. Skipping straight to the mock without the lessons is the fastest way to fail it.

Treating the knowledge check as a formality instead of a real self-test
Ignoring the terminal and labs — hands-on reps are where durable skill comes from

lessons.title: CLF-C02 exam Strategy: How to Win
concepts: The CLF-C02 exam rewards applied understanding over memorization — every domain here maps to something you will actually be asked to do
Time management wins: in timed assessments, bank the easy wins first, flag the hard ones, and never leave a question blank
Wrong answers are data: each missed scenario reveals a specific gap. Log it, revisit the lesson, and re-attempt until the pattern clicks
Sleep and spacing beat cramming: 90-minute focused sessions with breaks outperform marathon sessions, especially the week before clf-c02 exam day

The 3-pass method for timed assessments:
  Pass 1 (40% of time): answer everything you know cold
  Pass 2 (40% of time): work the flagged mediums with evidence
  Pass 3 (20% of time): educated guesses on the rest

Never spend 10 minutes on one question while five easy ones wait.

Perfectionism on one hard question while easy points expire
Studying new material the night before instead of reviewing what you know

lessons.title: EC2: Virtual Servers in the Cloud
concepts: EC2 provides resizable virtual servers: you choose the instance type (compute, memory, storage optimized), the AMI (OS image), and the network placement
You manage the OS and above: patching the guest OS, installing applications, and configuring the instance firewall (security groups) are YOUR responsibility
Instance families encode tradeoffs: C (compute), M (balanced), R/X (memory), P/G (GPU), I/D (storage) — match the family to the workload's bottleneck
EC2 is zonal: an instance lives in one Availability Zone; multi-AZ architectures need multiple instances behind a load balancer

example.code:
Launch checklist:
  AMI: Amazon Linux 2023
  Type: t3.medium (burstable, general purpose)
  AZ: us-east-1a (with a twin in 1b for HA)
  Security group: 443 in from ALB only, SSH from bastion
  Storage: gp3 EBS, encrypted

Every choice maps to an exam concept.
example.walkthrough: EC2's flexibility is its exam trap: questions test whether you know what YOU manage versus AWS. On EC2, the OS, patches, and app security are always yours — that never changes regardless of instance type.

pitfalls: Assuming AWS patches your EC2 guest OS — it does not
One instance in one AZ called 'highly available'
Picking instance types by vCPU alone — family matters more
lessons.try_it: For a web app needing 99.99% uptime, sketch the EC2 architecture: AZs, load balancer, instance count.

lessons.title: EC2 Pricing Models
concepts: On-Demand: pay per second, no commitment — for spiky, unpredictable, or short-lived workloads where flexibility beats discount
Reserved Instances and Savings Plans: 1- or 3-year commitments for up to 72% off — for steady-state workloads you can predict; Savings Plans are the flexible modern form
Spot Instances: bid on spare capacity for up to 90% off — for fault-tolerant, interruptible work (batch, CI) that survives 2-minute interruption notices
Dedicated Hosts/Instances: single-tenant hardware — for compliance or licensing (BYOL) needs, at a premium over shared tenancy

example.code:
Workload -> pricing:
  Web fleet, steady 24/7 -> Savings Plan (3-yr, ~60% off)
  Nightly batch renders -> Spot (up to 90% off)
  Month-end close, 3 days -> On-Demand
  Oracle DB, license tied to cores -> Dedicated Host

Match commitment to predictability.
example.walkthrough: The exam loves the 'which pricing model' question: the discriminator is always workload predictability + interruptibility. Steady = commit; spiky = On-Demand; interruptible = Spot; compliance = Dedicated.

pitfalls: Spot for a production database — interruption = outage
On-Demand for a flat 24/7 workload — paying 2-3x for no reason
Confusing Reserved Instances with Savings Plans flexibility
lessons.try_it: Classify four workloads you know: which EC2 pricing model each, and why?

lessons.title: Lambda: Serverless Functions
concepts: Lambda runs code without servers: upload the function, AWS handles provisioning, scaling, and patching — you pay per request plus GB-seconds of execution
Event-driven by design: triggers from S3 uploads, API Gateway, DynamoDB streams, schedules — Lambda shines at glue logic between services
15-minute maximum execution: Lambda is for short tasks, not long batch jobs — and cold starts add latency to infrequent invocations
Scales automatically but not infinitely: concurrency limits and downstream throttling (e.g., a database) are the real-world constraints

example.code:
Lambda fit test:
  Thumbnail on S3 upload -> YES (event, <1s)
  REST API backend -> YES (API Gateway trigger)
  6-hour video transcode -> NO (15-min limit; use Batch/Fargate)
  Cron report, 2 min -> YES (EventBridge schedule)

Duration decides.
example.walkthrough: Lambda's exam angle is always the tradeoff: no server management and automatic scaling versus execution limits, cold starts, and pay-per-invocation math that punishes constant high-volume workloads (where EC2 or Fargate wins).

pitfalls: Lambda for long-running jobs — the 15-minute wall
Ignoring cold starts on latency-sensitive APIs
Forgetting downstream limits — Lambda scales, your database may not
lessons.try_it: Name one workload perfect for Lambda and one terrible for it. What decides?

lessons.title: Containers: ECS, EKS, and Fargate
concepts: Containers package app + dependencies: consistent from laptop to cloud — Docker images run on ECS (AWS-native orchestrator) or EKS (managed Kubernetes)
ECS vs EKS: ECS is simpler and AWS-integrated; EKS is Kubernetes-standard for teams with K8s skills or multi-cloud portability needs
Fargate removes the servers: run containers without managing EC2 instances — pay per vCPU/memory-second; the serverless option for containers
EC2 launch type vs Fargate: EC2 gives control (and management burden); Fargate gives simplicity at a price premium for constant workloads

example.code:
Choice map:
  Team knows K8s, needs portability -> EKS
  AWS-native microservices, simple ops -> ECS + Fargate
  Constant high utilization, cost focus -> ECS on EC2
  Batch container jobs -> Fargate (no idle servers)

Skills + utilization decide.
example.walkthrough: Exam questions test the managed-vs-self-managed line: EKS manages the control plane (you still manage worker nodes unless Fargate); ECS + Fargate manages everything. Know exactly which layer AWS owns in each option.

pitfalls: EKS chosen with no Kubernetes expertise on the team
Fargate for 24/7 maxed-out containers — EC2 launch type is cheaper
Thinking containers remove all server management (EC2 launch type does not)
lessons.try_it: Your team ships microservices, no K8s skills, spiky traffic: ECS, EKS, or Fargate? Why?

lessons.title: Elastic Beanstalk and Lightsail
concepts: Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS: upload code, AWS provisions and manages the EC2, load balancer, and database plumbing — fastest path from code to running app
You keep full control underneath: Beanstalk environments expose the EC2 instances and settings — unlike pure serverless, you can SSH in and tune
Lightsail is simplified VPS: flat-rate virtual servers, databases, and storage for simple projects — predictable pricing, limited scaling
Exam positioning: Beanstalk = 'deploy code quickly without managing infrastructure'; Lightsail = 'simple, predictable, small-scale'

example.code:
PaaS decision:
  'Just run my code, handle the infra' -> Beanstalk
  'Simple VPS, fixed $5/mo budget' -> Lightsail
  'I need container orchestration' -> ECS
  'Event-driven micro-billing' -> Lambda

Abstraction level matches the ask.
example.walkthrough: Do not confuse Beanstalk with Lambda: Beanstalk runs long-lived servers (your code on EC2 it manages); Lambda runs short functions. 'Upload code and forget servers' describes both — the difference is duration and control.

pitfalls: Beanstalk for event-driven short tasks — Lambda fits better
Lightsail for auto-scaling enterprise workloads — it does not scale that way
Thinking Beanstalk locks you out of the infrastructure
lessons.try_it: A startup needs a blog + small store, fixed budget, no ops team: Beanstalk or Lightsail?

lessons.title: RDS: Managed Relational Databases
concepts: RDS runs MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, and SQL Server without the undifferentiated labor: AWS patches the OS and DB, backs up automatically, and handles failover
Multi-AZ for availability: a standby replica in another AZ with automatic failover — for production uptime, not performance
Read Replicas for scale: async copies that absorb read traffic (and can promote) — for performance, not failover speed
You still own the data and access: schema design, query tuning, user credentials, and encryption choices remain yours

example.code:
RDS decision:
  Need HA for the orders DB? -> Multi-AZ
  Reads overwhelming the primary? -> Read Replicas (up to 5)
  Engine choice? -> workload + license (Postgres/MySQL = open)
  Backups? -> automated, 7-day default retention

HA and scale are separate knobs.
example.walkthrough: The exam's favorite RDS trap is Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas: Multi-AZ is a standby you cannot read from (availability); Read Replicas serve reads (performance). Mixing them up fails the question every time.

pitfalls: Multi-AZ for read scaling — the standby takes no traffic
Read Replicas for fast failover — they are async and laggy
Assuming RDS tunes your queries — performance is still yours
lessons.try_it: An RDS primary is read-saturated at peak: Multi-AZ, Read Replica, or bigger instance? Why?

lessons.title: Aurora: Cloud-Native Relational
concepts: Aurora is AWS's cloud-native relational engine: MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible with up to 5x/3x the throughput of stock engines
Storage auto-scales to 128 TB and replicates 6 ways across 3 AZs — storage-level high availability without standby instances
Up to 15 low-latency read replicas with millisecond failover priority tiers — read scaling far beyond RDS's 5
Aurora Global Database spans regions with <1s replication lag — for global apps needing low-latency reads worldwide

example.code:
Aurora vs RDS:
  Highest perf + auto-scaling storage -> Aurora
  Oracle/SQL Server needed -> RDS (Aurora lacks them)
  Global reads, <1s lag -> Aurora Global
  Cheapest simple MySQL -> RDS MySQL

Aurora wins on scale; RDS on engine breadth.
example.walkthrough: Remember the compatibility story: Aurora speaks MySQL and PostgreSQL wire protocols, so migrations are often driver-level changes — but it is NOT bit-identical, so test. The exam tests 'which engine options' frequently.

pitfalls: Aurora for Oracle workloads — unsupported engine
Assuming 6-way storage replication means no backups needed
Choosing RDS when the workload needs 15 read replicas
lessons.try_it: A global SaaS needs Postgres compatibility and fast regional reads: Aurora or RDS?

lessons.title: DynamoDB: Serverless NoSQL
concepts: DynamoDB is serverless key-value/document NoSQL: single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, no servers to manage
Two capacity modes: Provisioned (you set read/write units — cheaper for predictable traffic) and On-Demand (pay per request — for spiky or new workloads)
DAX adds in-memory caching for microsecond reads; Global Tables replicate multi-region active-active for global apps
Design is access-pattern-first: model your partition keys around your queries — DynamoDB punishes relational thinking (no joins, no ad-hoc SQL)

example.code:
DynamoDB fit:
  Session store, ms latency -> YES
  Spiky new app, unknown traffic -> On-Demand
  Steady 10k reads/s -> Provisioned (cheaper)
  Complex reporting queries -> NO (use RDS/Redshift)

Keys first, queries second.
example.walkthrough: The exam tests DynamoDB's boundaries: it is not a relational database and not a data warehouse. 'Needs joins and complex queries' always points away from DynamoDB — usually to RDS or Redshift.

pitfalls: Using DynamoDB for analytical reporting — wrong tool
On-Demand for flat predictable traffic — overpaying
Relational schema design ported directly — hot partitions
lessons.try_it: Shopping cart sessions, 50k writes/sec, global users: DynamoDB mode and features?

lessons.title: Purpose-Built: ElastiCache, Redshift, Neptune, DocumentDB
concepts: ElastiCache: managed Redis/Memcached in-memory caching — microsecond reads in front of RDS/DynamoDB; Redis adds pub/sub and persistence
Redshift: petabyte-scale data warehouse for OLAP analytics — columnar storage, massively parallel queries; NOT for transactional workloads
Neptune: managed graph database — fraud detection, knowledge graphs, relationship-heavy queries that SQL struggles with
DocumentDB: MongoDB-compatible document store — for teams with MongoDB codebases wanting a managed AWS home

example.code:
Database picker:
  Cache hot reads -> ElastiCache (Redis)
  Petabyte analytics -> Redshift
  'Friends of friends' queries -> Neptune
  Existing MongoDB app -> DocumentDB
  Transactions + joins -> RDS/Aurora

One workload, one purpose-built store.
example.walkthrough: CLF-C02 loves the purpose-built lineup: each service maps to a workload adjective — in-memory, warehouse-scale, graph, document. Learn the one-line 'when to use' for each and the exam's database questions become free points.

pitfalls: Redshift for order transactions — OLTP on an OLAP store
ElastiCache as the system of record — cache is not storage
Neptune for simple key-value — DynamoDB is cheaper and simpler
lessons.try_it: Match four workloads (leaderboard cache, sales analytics, fraud graph, mobile backend) to services.

lessons.title: DMS and Database Migration
concepts: AWS DMS migrates databases with minimal downtime: homogeneous (Oracle→Oracle) or heterogeneous (Oracle→Aurora PostgreSQL) with ongoing replication
AWS SCT converts schemas and code: translates Oracle PL/SQL or SQL Server T-SQL to the target engine — DMS moves data, SCT moves logic
Minimal-downtime pattern: DMS replicates continuously, then cut over in a short window — the production database stays live during migration
Exam framing: 'migrate a database to AWS with least downtime' → DMS; 'convert schema from Oracle to Postgres' → DMS + SCT

example.code:
Migration flow:
  1. SCT: assess + convert schema/code
  2. DMS: full load + change-data-capture replication
  3. Validate: row counts, checksums, app tests
  4. Cutover: stop writes, final sync, flip connection

Assess, replicate, validate, cut over.
example.walkthrough: DMS replicates data, not everything: large objects, some data types, and secondary indexes need attention — and the source stays the authority until cutover. The exam keeps it simple: DMS = move data, SCT = convert schema.

pitfalls: Expecting DMS to rewrite application SQL — that is SCT + dev work
Cutting over without validation — silent data gaps
One-shot dump/restore when downtime is unacceptable
lessons.try_it: Migrate Oracle on-prem to Aurora PostgreSQL, <5 min downtime: which services, what order?

lessons.title: Capstone: Cloud Architecture Project — Overview
concepts: Your capstone: a production-ready AWS architecture: multi-AZ compute, managed database, cost model, and a Well-Architected review
Break the build into phases: plan, build, secure, validate, document. Each phase maps to domains in this bootcamp
Document as you go — your write-up is the interview artifact that proves senior-level ownership
Done beats perfect: a working system with honest limitations beats an unfinished ambitious one

example.code:
Phase 1: Design the architecture: VPC, compute, database, and CDN for a 3-tier web app
Phase 2: Apply shared responsibility: document what AWS owns vs what you own at each layer
Phase 3: Model the cost: pricing calculator estimate with On-Demand vs Savings Plans analysis
Phase 4: Secure it: IAM roles, security groups, encryption, and CloudTrail logging
Phase 5: Review against the Well-Architected Framework's six pillars and remediate gaps
example.walkthrough: Treat each phase as a mini-project with a definition of done. Demo each phase working before moving on — integration surprises compound.

pitfalls: Starting to build before writing the plan — an hour of planning saves ten of rework
Skipping documentation until the end — you will forget why decisions were made
Gold-plating phase one while phase four remains untouched
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph project plan: what you will build, in what phases, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Capstone: Validation and Demo
concepts: Validate every requirement with a test you can show: screenshots, command output, or a live demo
Prepare the 5-minute demo narrative: problem, approach, build, validation, lessons learned
Anticipate questions: know the trade-offs you made and what you would do with more time
Publish the write-up: architecture diagram, build log, validation evidence, reflection

example.code:
Demo script template:
  1. The problem (30s)
  2. Architecture overview (60s)
  3. Live walkthrough (2 min)
  4. Validation evidence (60s)
  5. What I would do next (30s)
example.walkthrough: A demo that only shows the happy path invites the hardest questions. Show one failure mode and how the system handles it — that is what interviewers remember.

pitfalls: Demoing without rehearsing — run it three times end-to-end first
Hiding limitations — name them before you are asked
No architecture diagram — draw the system before you demo it
lessons.try_it: Draft your 5-minute demo script for the capstone project.

lessons.title: Athena: SQL on S3
concepts: Athena runs standard SQL directly against data in S3 — no servers, no loading: define the table schema, point at the bucket, and query
Serverless and pay-per-query: you pay for the data scanned ($5/TB), so partitioning and columnar formats (Parquet) slash the bill
Best for ad-hoc exploration: log analysis, one-off investigations, and occasional reporting — not for dashboards hit 1000x a day
Integrates with Glue Data Catalog for table definitions and QuickSight for visualization

example.code:
Cost math:
  1 TB CSV scanned per query x 20 queries/day
  = $100/day. Convert to Parquet + partition by date:
  50 GB scanned per query -> $5/day.

Format is pricing.
example.walkthrough: Athena's exam trap is the 'data scanned' pricing: every question about Athena cost optimization answers with partitioning, compression, and columnar formats. Unpartitioned CSV is the expensive wrong answer.

pitfalls: Querying raw CSV dumps repeatedly — maximum scan cost
Athena for high-QPS dashboards — use Redshift or cached aggregates
No partitioning on time-series data
lessons.try_it: Your Athena bill tripled: name three changes that cut data scanned per query.

lessons.title: EMR: Big Data Processing
concepts: EMR runs Hadoop, Spark, and Presto clusters: petabyte-scale batch processing, machine learning prep, and large ETL jobs
Managed but not serverless: you choose instance types and counts — EMR handles provisioning, patching, and framework setup
Transient clusters are the cost trick: spin up for the job, terminate after — you pay only for processing time, not idle clusters
Exam contrast: EMR = big batch frameworks you manage at cluster level; Glue = serverless ETL you do not manage

example.code:
EMR vs Glue:
  Nightly 2 TB Spark job, custom libs -> EMR transient
  Daily CSV -> Parquet ETL -> Glue (serverless)
  Ad-hoc SQL on logs -> Athena
  Streaming clickstream -> Kinesis + Firehose

Framework + duration decide.
example.walkthrough: Do not pick EMR for small data: the cluster overhead (spin-up time, minimum sizing) makes it the slow expensive choice under ~100 GB. The exam tests 'right-sized analytics' — match the engine to the data volume.

pitfalls: EMR for 10 GB datasets — cluster overhead dominates
24/7 EMR cluster for a nightly 1-hour job — use transient
Confusing EMR (frameworks) with Redshift (warehouse SQL)
lessons.try_it: 2 TB nightly Spark ETL, custom Python libs: EMR or Glue? What cluster pattern?

lessons.title: Glue: Serverless ETL and Data Catalog
concepts: Glue is serverless ETL: visually or code-authored jobs that extract, transform, and load data — no clusters to manage
Glue Data Catalog is the metadata hub: table definitions shared by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR — define once, query everywhere
Crawlers auto-discover schema: point a crawler at S3 and it infers tables — the fastest path from raw dumps to queryable data
Pay per DPU-second: cost follows actual processing — ideal for scheduled or event-driven ETL that does not justify a standing cluster

example.code:
Glue pipeline:
  S3 raw CSV -> Crawler (catalog) -> Glue job (clean + Parquet)
  -> S3 curated -> Athena/QuickSight

Catalog once, consume everywhere.
example.walkthrough: Glue's exam identity is 'serverless + catalog': any question pairing ETL with 'no infrastructure to manage' or mentioning the Data Catalog points to Glue. Crawlers are the giveaway keyword for schema discovery.

pitfalls: Hand-writing DDL for 500 evolving CSV dumps — use a crawler
Glue for sub-second streaming — use Kinesis
Rebuilding table definitions per service — use the shared Catalog
lessons.try_it: Raw CSVs land in S3 hourly; analysts need clean Parquet by morning: sketch the Glue flow.

lessons.title: Kinesis: Real-Time Streaming
concepts: Kinesis Data Streams: real-time ingestion of clickstreams, IoT telemetry, and logs — producers write, consumers process in order per shard
Amazon Data Firehose: the zero-admin loader — streams land in S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch with batching, compression, and format conversion built in
Streams vs Firehose: Streams = you manage consumers and scaling (full control); Firehose = managed delivery to destinations (simplicity)
Exam heuristic: 'real-time analytics with custom processing' → Data Streams; 'load streaming data into S3/Redshift easily' → Firehose

example.code:
Streaming choice:
  Fraud detection, custom per-event logic -> Data Streams
  Clickstream -> S3 data lake, no custom code -> Firehose
  IoT -> OpenSearch dashboards -> Firehose
  Ordered per-user event processing -> Data Streams (shard per user)

Custom logic decides.
example.walkthrough: Shards are the scaling unit of Data Streams: each shard gives ~1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out — throughput planning is shard math. The exam rarely goes this deep, but 'res hard per shard' separates Streams from the fully-managed Firehose.

pitfalls: Firehose when custom per-record processing is required
Data Streams for simple S3 delivery — overkill
No shard planning on high-throughput Streams
lessons.try_it: IoT sensors stream 5k events/sec to S3 for Athena queries: Streams or Firehose? Why?

lessons.title: QuickSight and the Analytics Pipeline
concepts: QuickSight is serverless BI: dashboards and visualizations with pay-per-session pricing — no BI servers to run
SPICE (in-memory engine) accelerates dashboards: import data for fast queries; direct query for live data — speed vs freshness tradeoff
The full pipeline: ingest (Kinesis/Firehose, DMS) → store (S3 data lake, Redshift) → catalog (Glue) → analyze (Athena/EMR) → visualize (QuickSight)
Exam view: QuickSight = 'dashboards without servers'; know its place at the END of the pipeline, consuming from S3, Athena, RDS, or Redshift

example.code:
Pipeline map:
  Sources -> [Firehose/DMS] -> S3 lake
  S3 lake -> [Glue catalog] -> Athena (ad-hoc)
  S3 lake -> Redshift (heavy BI)
  Athena/Redshift -> QuickSight dashboards

Each stage has one job.
example.walkthrough: Place every analytics service on the pipeline before memorizing features: ingestion, storage, catalog, processing, visualization. CLF-C02 questions describe a STAGE ('we need dashboards') — the service follows from the stage.

pitfalls: QuickSight querying raw CSV in S3 directly at scale — curate first
Building the pipeline backwards from the dashboard
One service doing every stage — pipeline thinking wins
lessons.try_it: Draw the 5-stage pipeline for 'clickstream to executive dashboard' naming the AWS service per stage.

lessons.title: The 6 Rs of Migration
concepts: Rehost ('lift and shift'): move as-is to EC2 — fastest, least change, but brings old inefficiencies to the cloud
Replatform ('lift and reshape'): small optimizations during the move (RDS instead of self-managed DB) — the pragmatic middle
Repurchase: drop the old app for SaaS — move to a different product entirely (e.g., on-prem CRM → cloud CRM)
Refactor/Re-architect: rebuild cloud-native (microservices, serverless) — highest effort, highest long-term payoff; Retain: keep on-premises (for now); Retire: turn it off

example.code:
R-picker:
  500 VMs, deadline 6 months -> Rehost, then optimize
  Self-managed DB, team tired of patching -> Replatform to RDS
  Old ticket system, SaaS exists -> Repurchase
  Monolith blocking releases -> Refactor (phase 2)

Deadlines pick the R.
example.walkthrough: The exam's R questions always hinge on constraints: tight deadline + minimal change = Rehost; willing to change for managed benefits = Replatform; 'move to SaaS' in the stem = Repurchase. Read the constraint, not the technology.

pitfalls: Refactoring everything under a 6-month deadline — the classic failure
Rehosting and declaring victory — no optimization ever follows
Repurchase confused with Replatform
lessons.try_it: A factory has 200 VMs and 9 months to exit the data center: which R, and what is phase 2?

lessons.title: AWS CAF: The Migration Framework
concepts: The Cloud Adoption Framework organizes migration into 6 perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, Operations — migration is not just servers
Business perspective: the business case — TCO comparison, value metrics, and stakeholder alignment before any technical work
People perspective: roles, skills, and training — the team must be able to operate what you migrate to
Security and Governance perspectives: compliance, risk, and controls travel WITH the workloads — they are not phase 2

example.code:
CAF check:
  Business: TCO model approved? [ ]
  People: cloud skills plan? [ ]
  Governance: cost controls? [ ]
  Platform: landing zone ready? [ ]
  Security: controls mapped? [ ]
  Operations: runbooks updated? [ ]

Six boxes, all checked.
example.walkthrough: CAF questions test breadth: the wrong answers focus only on technology. If a scenario mentions skills gaps, compliance, or cost governance, the answer lives in the non-technical perspectives.

pitfalls: Treating migration as a pure infrastructure project
Skipping the business case — migrating without knowing why
Security as an afterthought instead of a perspective
lessons.try_it: A migration stalled on 'nobody knows who approves cloud spend': which CAF perspective failed?

lessons.title: Migration Tools: DMS, MGN, and DataSync
concepts: Application Migration Service (MGN): lift-and-shift for servers — replicates EC2/VMs continuously and cuts over with minimal downtime; the Rehost workhorse
DMS: database migration with ongoing replication (plus SCT for schema conversion) — the data-layer counterpart to MGN
DataSync: fast, managed data transfer — NFS/SMB/HDFS to S3/EFS/FSx, with scheduling, validation, and bandwidth control
Exam mapping: servers with minimal downtime → MGN; databases → DMS; file shares at speed → DataSync

example.code:
Tool picker:
  300 VMs, minimal downtime -> MGN
  Oracle DB -> Aurora -> DMS + SCT
  50 TB file share -> S3 -> DataSync
  5 PB datacenter exit -> Snowball/Snowmobile

Workload type picks the tool.
example.walkthrough: Keep MGN (servers) and DMS (databases) surgically separate in your head: the exam deliberately pairs a server-migration scenario with DMS as a distractor. Servers → MGN; databases → DMS — no exceptions.

pitfalls: DMS for server lift-and-shift — wrong tool
MGN for database migration — wrong tool
Manual rsync for 50 TB — DataSync exists for this
lessons.try_it: 200 VMs + Oracle DB, minimal downtime: which two services, and what does each move?

lessons.title: Snow Family: Moving Data at Scale
concepts: Snowcone: small, portable edge device (8 TB) — rugged collection and edge compute where networks are poor
Snowball: 80 TB per device, clustered for petabyte moves — the workhorse for 'too big for the network' transfers
Snowmobile: a literal truck — exabyte-scale datacenter evacuation when even Snowballs would take too long
Rule of thumb: under ~100 TB with good bandwidth → network (Direct Connect/DataSync); beyond that → Snow; beyond petabytes → Snowmobile

example.code:
Transfer math:
  500 TB over 1 Gbps ≈ 46 days -> Snowball fleet
  500 TB over 10 Gbps ≈ 4.6 days -> DataSync/Direct Connect
  8 EB datacenter -> Snowmobile

Bandwidth x time decides.
example.walkthrough: The exam's Snow questions are math-free but logic-heavy: 'limited connectivity' or 'petabytes' in the stem = Snow family; the device size in the answers distinguishes Cone/Ball/Mobile. Read for scale words.

pitfalls: Snowball for 500 GB — network is faster and cheaper
Network transfer for 5 PB over 1 Gbps — do the math
Forgetting Snowcone's edge-compute role
lessons.try_it: A ship generates 20 TB/voyage with no connectivity at sea: which Snow device, and why?

lessons.title: Migration Strategies and Landing Zones
concepts: Land well first: a landing zone (via Control Tower) gives every migration guardrails — accounts, SSO, logging, and SCPs — before the first workload moves
Wave planning: migrate in waves by dependency (low-risk, low-dependency first) — each wave proves the pattern for the next
The 3-phase rhythm: Assess (discover, TCO, R-select) → Mobilize (landing zone, skills, pilot) → Migrate & Modernize (waves, then optimize)
Post-migration is not done: decommission the old, validate the bills against the TCO model, and schedule the Replatform/Refactor phase Rehost deferred

example.code:
Wave plan:
  Wave 0: landing zone + pilot (1 app)
  Wave 1: independent dev/test (20 apps)
  Wave 2: production, low dependency (50 apps)
  Wave 3: complex/coupled (remaining)

Prove, then scale.
example.walkthrough: Migrations fail on dependencies, not technology: discover application dependencies BEFORE wave planning (Migration Evaluator/Application Discovery Service), or wave 2 will drag wave 1's databases along with it.

pitfalls: Migrating without dependency discovery — coupling surprises
No landing zone — every team invents its own guardrails
Declaring victory at cutover — optimization never happens
lessons.try_it: Sketch waves 0-2 for a 100-app estate with a tangled ERP core: what moves when?

lessons.title: The Six Pillars
concepts: Operational Excellence: run and monitor systems to deliver business value — IaC, small reversible changes, learn from failure
Security: protect data and systems — least privilege, encryption everywhere, automate security, traceability
Reliability: recover from failure — auto-recovery, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity, test recovery

Performance Efficiency: use resources efficiently — right-sizing, experimentation, mechanical sympathy; Cost Optimization: avoid waste — pay-as-you-go, measure efficiency; Sustainability: minimize environmental impact

example.code:
Pillar one-liners:
  Ops: run it well, change it safely
  Security: least privilege + encryption + automation
  Reliability: survive failure automatically
  Performance: right resource, right job
  Cost: pay for value, kill waste
  Sustainability: efficient = green

Six lenses, one architecture.
example.walkthrough: Exam questions describe a PRACTICE and ask for the pillar: 'automated backups and multi-AZ' → Reliability; 'MFA and encryption' → Security; 'turning off idle resources' → Cost Optimization. Learn the practice-to-pillar mapping.

pitfalls: Memorizing pillar names without their practices
One pillar to the exclusion of others — tradeoffs are the point
Treating Sustainability as optional — it is a scored pillar
lessons.try_it: Take three practices (auto-scaling, KMS encryption, Savings Plans) and name each pillar.

lessons.title: Security Pillar Design Principles
concepts: Strong identity foundation: centralize identity, enforce MFA, use temporary credentials (roles) over long-lived keys
Least privilege and traceability: grant only needed permissions; log everything (CloudTrail) so actions are auditable
Security at every layer: defense in depth — edge (WAF/Shield), network (security groups), compute (patching), data (encryption)
Automate security: guardrails as code (Config rules, SCPs), secrets in Secrets Manager — humans should not hand-handle credentials

example.code:
Security checklist:
  [ ] MFA on root + IAM users
  [ ] Roles, not access keys, for apps
  [ ] Encryption at rest (KMS) + in transit (TLS)
  [ ] CloudTrail enabled, logs immutable
  [ ] Security groups deny-by-default

Automate every line.
example.walkthrough: The exam's security questions reward the strictest correct option: given a choice between 'open security group to the world' convenience and least-privilege, the Framework always picks least privilege — even when it is more work.

pitfalls: Long-lived access keys embedded in applications
Security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 'temporarily'
Manual security reviews instead of Config rules
lessons.try_it: Audit a hypothetical app: list 5 security-pillar violations and their fixes.

lessons.title: Reliability Pillar Design Principles
concepts: Automatic recovery: design for failure — health checks, auto-restart, and failover that needs no human at 3 AM
Scale horizontally: add more small units instead of bigger ones — AZ distribution plus load balancing over vertical scaling
Stop guessing capacity: auto-scaling on demand signals beats provisioned-for-peak waste and provisioned-for-average outages
Test recovery: game days and chaos drills — untested failover is a hope, and hope is not a pillar

example.code:
Reliability patterns:
  EC2 -> Auto Scaling group across 3 AZs
  RDS -> Multi-AZ with automated backups
  Static -> S3 + CloudFront (11 9s durability)
  Queue -> SQS decouples, absorbs spikes

Every tier survives a failure.
example.walkthrough: Reliability questions hinge on automation: the Framework prefers the answer where recovery happens WITHOUT human intervention. 'An operator fails over manually' is always the wrong answer next to 'automated failover.'

pitfalls: Single AZ deployments called 'reliable'
Manual failover runbooks as the HA strategy
Vertical scaling as the growth plan
lessons.try_it: Design the reliability story for a 3-tier app: what fails, what recovers automatically?

lessons.title: Cost Optimization Pillar
concepts: Pay only for what you use: right-size instances, delete unattached EBS volumes and idle load balancers — waste is the default without hygiene
Measure efficiency: Cost Explorer, Compute Optimizer rightsizing recommendations, and per-team cost allocation tags
Commit where predictable: Savings Plans/RIs for steady state; Spot for interruptible; On-Demand nowhere long-term
Design for cost: serverless and auto-scaling align cost with demand — the cheapest resource is the one that does not exist when idle

example.code:
Cost hygiene loop (monthly):
  1. Cost Explorer: top 5 services by spend
  2. Compute Optimizer: rightsizing actions
  3. Trusted Advisor: idle resources
  4. Tag compliance: 100% of spend attributed
  5. Commit review: coverage vs usage

Waste compounds; so does hygiene.
example.walkthrough: Cost questions test the 'cheapest correct' instinct: the Framework never picks the expensive easy answer when a cheaper managed answer exists. But 'cheapest' never means 'less reliable than the requirement' — requirements bound the optimization.

pitfalls: On-Demand forever on flat workloads
Untagged spend nobody owns
Idle resources 'in case we need them'
lessons.try_it: Run the monthly cost hygiene loop on a hypothetical $20k/mo bill: where is the waste?

lessons.title: Performance Efficiency and Sustainability
concepts: Performance: select the right resource types (compute/memory/GPU families), use serverless to remove idle, and experiment — benchmark, do not guess
Mechanical sympathy: understand the underlying tech — EBS volume types, S3 request rates, database indexing — and design WITH it, not against it
Sustainability: utilization is the lever — higher utilization means fewer resources for the same work; managed and serverless services maximize it
The shared model: efficient architectures are BOTH cheaper and greener — Cost Optimization and Sustainability usually agree

example.code:
Efficiency wins:
  Graviton instances: 40% better price-performance
  Auto-scaling: no idle over-provisioning
  S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic cost fit
  Right region: closer = faster + less transfer

Efficiency compounds across pillars.
example.walkthrough: Sustainability questions are the exam's newest favorite: the answers always involve utilization, managed services, and efficient instance types (Graviton). 'Run idle servers just in case' fails both cost AND sustainability.

pitfalls: Guessing instance types instead of benchmarking
Idle over-provisioning 'for headroom'
Ignoring Graviton price-performance
lessons.try_it: Name three changes that improve cost AND sustainability simultaneously.

lessons.title: Cloud Deployment Models
concepts: Public cloud: everything on AWS — maximum elasticity, no data centers; the default the exam assumes
Hybrid: mix of on-premises and cloud — for gradual migration, data residency, or latency-sensitive systems (with Outposts/Direct Connect bridging)
Private cloud/on-premises: dedicated infrastructure you operate — maximum control, zero elasticity; the exam contrasts this against cloud economics
The exam discriminator is always the constraint: 'must keep data on-premises' → hybrid/private; 'no infrastructure to manage' → public cloud

example.code:
Model picker:
  Startup, global users, no DC -> public cloud
  Bank, trading engine <1ms from exchange -> hybrid (on-prem + cloud burst)
  Classified data, air-gapped law -> private/on-prem
  5-year migration -> hybrid, shrinking on-prem

Constraint picks the model.
example.walkthrough: Hybrid is not a failure state: the exam treats it as a legitimate architecture for real constraints (latency, sovereignty, sunk investment). Do not reflexively answer 'move everything to cloud' when the stem names a constraint.

pitfalls: Public cloud for legally air-gapped data — compliance violation
Private cloud chosen for 'elasticity' — it has none
Ignoring the constraint words in the scenario stem
lessons.try_it: A hospital must keep patient images on-premises by law but wants cloud analytics: which model?

lessons.title: The Six Advantages of Cloud
concepts: Trade capital expense for variable expense: no data-center build-outs — pay for what you use, when you use it
Benefit from massive economies of scale: AWS's purchasing power becomes your lower per-unit cost
Stop guessing capacity: scale up and down on demand instead of provisioning for the peak you might never hit
Increase speed and agility, stop spending money running data centers, and go global in minutes — the other three the exam lists verbatim

example.code:
Advantage matcher:
  'We over-provisioned 3x for Black Friday' -> stop guessing capacity
  'Deploy to Sydney took 9 months' -> go global in minutes
  '$2M datacenter refresh due' -> trade capex for variable

Memorize all six; the exam quotes them.
example.walkthrough: These six are rote-memorization points: the exam asks them nearly verbatim. Write them from memory until automatic — they are the cheapest points on the test.

pitfalls: Knowing three of the six — the exam tests all of them
Paraphrasing loosely — learn the official phrasings
Confusing advantages with deployment models
lessons.try_it: Write all six advantages from memory. Which two did you miss?

lessons.title: Global Infrastructure: Regions, AZs, and Edge
concepts: Region: a geographic area with multiple isolated Availability Zones — choose regions for latency, compliance, and service availability
Availability Zone: one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking — the unit of failure isolation
Edge locations: CloudFront/Route 53 points of presence in 400+ cities — content cached close to users; NOT full regions
Local Zones and Wavelength extend regions for ultra-low-latency needs (gaming, 5G) — exam depth stops at 'they exist for latency'

example.code:
Geography drill:
  Deploy for EU data residency -> eu-west-1 (Ireland)
  Survive a datacenter fire -> 2+ AZs in one region
  Fast static content in 400 cities -> CloudFront edge locations
  5G app, <10ms -> Wavelength zone

Scope matches the need.
example.walkthrough: The classic confusion is Region vs AZ vs Edge: Regions hold AZs; AZs hold data centers; Edge locations hold caches. 'Deploy across AZs' ≠ 'deploy across regions' — the exam separates them deliberately.

pitfalls: Edge locations called 'regions' — they are not
One AZ called 'highly available'
Choosing regions by name familiarity instead of latency/compliance
lessons.try_it: Map: user in Tokyo, data must stay in Japan, survive AZ failure — what do you pick?

lessons.title: Security OF vs IN the Cloud
concepts: Security OF the cloud = AWS: physical facilities, hardware, network infrastructure, hypervisors, and managed-service software patching
Security IN the cloud = you: your data, IAM users and permissions, OS patching on EC2, security-group rules, and application security
The line moves with abstraction: EC2 → you own the OS; RDS → AWS patches the OS, you own the data and access; S3 → AWS owns everything below your bucket policies
Exam rule of thumb: the more managed the service, the more AWS owns — but your data and access control are ALWAYS yours

example.code:
Responsibility ladder:
  On-prem: you own everything
  EC2: AWS to hypervisor; you own OS+
  RDS: AWS to OS patch; you own data/access
  S3: AWS to infrastructure; you own policies/data
  SaaS: AWS owns most; you own users/data

Abstraction shifts the line upward.
example.walkthrough: Two things never move to AWS no matter the service: classification and protection of YOUR data, and who can access it (IAM). Every 'who is responsible for the data' question answers: the customer. Always.

pitfalls: Assuming managed services remove all customer responsibility
'AWS handles security' as a complete answer — OF vs IN matters
Forgetting the line moves with each service
lessons.try_it: For EC2, RDS, and S3: draw the responsibility line for OS patching, data encryption, and access control.

lessons.title: Your Responsibilities: Data and Access
concepts: Data classification and protection: you decide what is sensitive, encrypt it (KMS), and control its lifecycle — AWS provides the tools, you make the decisions
Identity and access management: creating IAM users/roles, enforcing MFA, applying least-privilege policies, and rotating credentials
Network configuration: security groups, NACLs, and VPC design — the firewall rules are yours to write (and to get wrong)
Application security: your code, your patches on EC2, your secrets management — the shared model never covers your bugs

example.code:
Customer checklist:
  [ ] Data classified; KMS encryption enabled
  [ ] IAM: MFA everywhere, least privilege, no root keys
  [ ] Security groups: deny-by-default, reviewed quarterly
  [ ] EC2 fleet: patched within SLA
  [ ] Secrets in Secrets Manager, never in code

Yours, end to end.
example.walkthrough: The exam punishes 'AWS will handle it' thinking about customer duties: leaked access keys, open S3 buckets, and unpatched EC2 are customer failures in the model — and in real breach reports.

pitfalls: Access keys in code repos — customer failure
S3 bucket open to the world — customer failure
Unpatched EC2 fleet — customer failure
lessons.try_it: A breach used a leaked IAM key with admin rights: whose responsibility failed, at which layer?

lessons.title: AWS Responsibilities: Foundation Up
concepts: Physical security: data-center access controls, guards, and hardware lifecycle — audited under SOC, ISO, PCI compliance programs
Hardware and virtualization: server maintenance, hypervisor patching, and network infrastructure — the floor your workloads stand on
Managed-service software: RDS OS/DB patching, Lambda runtime updates, S3 durability engineering (11 nines via replication)
Compliance of the platform: AWS maintains the certifications; you inherit them for the layers AWS manages (via Artifact reports)

example.code:
AWS owns:
  Concrete: buildings, guards, biometric access
  Metal: servers, disks, network gear
  Hypervisor: the virtualization layer
  Managed SW: RDS patches, Lambda runtimes
  Paper: SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS reports

Everything under your abstraction line.
example.walkthrough: Inheritance is the exam concept: you INHERIT AWS's compliance for the layers it manages, but you must still achieve compliance for YOUR layers. 'AWS is PCI certified' does not make your app PCI compliant.

pitfalls: 'AWS is compliant, so we are compliant' — inheritance has limits
Expecting AWS to patch your EC2 guest OS
Ignoring Artifact reports during audits
lessons.try_it: Your auditor asks for the hypervisor patch records: who provides them, from where?

lessons.title: Shared Controls and Edge Cases
concepts: Patch management is SHARED: AWS patches the hypervisor and managed services; you patch EC2 guests and containers — the exam's favorite split
Configuration management is shared: AWS provides Config/CloudTrail; you define the rules and respond to findings
Awareness and training: AWS secures the platform; you train your people — phishing your admins is not AWS's problem to solve
Service-specific edges: on S3 YOU configure bucket policies and encryption; on IAM YOU write every policy — managed does not mean automatic

example.code:
Edge-case answers:
  S3 bucket exposed? -> customer (bucket policy)
  RDS OS patch overdue? -> AWS (managed patching)
  EC2 OS patch overdue? -> customer
  DDoS absorbed? -> AWS Shield Standard (automatic)
  App SQL injection? -> customer (code)

Ask: whose hands configure it?
example.walkthrough: When stuck, ask 'whose hands touch the control?' — if you configure it (bucket policy, security group, IAM policy), it is yours; if it runs beneath your visibility (hypervisor, physical guards), it is AWS's. That heuristic resolves nearly every exam edge case.

pitfalls: Memorizing lists instead of the 'whose hands' heuristic
S3 encryption as 'AWS's job' — you must ENABLE it
DDoS protection assumed absent — Shield Standard is automatic
lessons.try_it: Classify five controls (WAF rules, hypervisor patches, S3 policies, MFA, AZ power) by owner.

lessons.title: Compute: EC2, Lambda, and Containers
concepts: EC2: resizable virtual servers you fully control — choose AMI, instance type, storage, and networking; you patch the OS
Lambda: serverless functions triggered by events — no servers, 15-minute max execution, pay per request and GB-second
Containers (ECS/EKS/Fargate): packaged apps with dependencies — ECS is AWS-native, EKS is managed Kubernetes, Fargate removes the servers
Exam mapping: 'full control of OS' → EC2; 'event-driven, no servers' → Lambda; 'same environment dev-to-prod' → containers

example.code:
Compute picker:
  Lift-and-shift VM fleet -> EC2
  S3 upload triggers thumbnail -> Lambda
  Microservices, team knows K8s -> EKS
  Microservices, no K8s skills -> ECS + Fargate
  'Just run my code' -> Elastic Beanstalk

Control vs convenience.
example.walkthrough: Duration is Lambda's hard exam boundary: anything over 15 minutes cannot be Lambda, full stop. When a scenario mentions hours-long processing, eliminate Lambda immediately.

pitfalls: Lambda for 2-hour batch jobs
EC2 when the ask is 'no server management'
EKS for a team with zero container experience
lessons.try_it: Classify: nightly 3-hour report, API webhook handler, 20 microservices — which compute each?

lessons.title: Storage: S3 Classes and EBS/EFS
concepts: S3 Standard: frequent access, 11-nines durability; Intelligent-Tiering: auto-moves by access pattern; Standard-IA/One Zone-IA: infrequent access
Glacier tiers: Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive — retrieval from milliseconds to 48 hours, priced by patience; Deep Archive is the cheapest storage in AWS
EBS: block storage for EC2 — gp3 (general), io2 (high IOPS), st1/sc1 (throughput/cold HDD); snapshots to S3 for backup
EFS: elastic NFS file system shared across instances/AZs — for shared file needs; Instance store is ephemeral (data lost on stop)

example.code:
Storage picker:
  Web assets, frequent -> S3 Standard
  7-year compliance logs -> Deep Archive
  DB volume, 10k IOPS -> io2
  Shared WordPress uploads -> EFS
  Temp scratch on EC2 -> instance store (ephemeral!)

Access pattern picks the class.
example.walkthrough: Durability vs availability vs retrieval time: S3 is 11-nines durable across ALL classes — the classes differ in AVAILABILITY and retrieval speed/cost. 'Durable archive, rarely accessed' screams Deep Archive, not Standard.

pitfalls: Glacier for frequently-accessed data — retrieval fees explode
Instance store for anything you cannot lose
EBS for sharing between instances — use EFS
lessons.try_it: Backups kept 7 years, retrieved maybe once: which S3 class, and what is the retrieval time?

lessons.title: Networking: VPC Essentials
concepts: VPC: your isolated network — you define CIDR, subnets (public/private per AZ), route tables, and gateways
Internet Gateway: public subnets reach the internet; NAT Gateway: private subnets reach OUT (updates) without being reachable IN
Security groups: stateful instance firewalls (return traffic auto-allowed); NACLs: stateless subnet firewalls (explicit both directions)
Exam contrast: stateful vs stateless is THE security-group-vs-NACL question — memorize it cold

example.code:
VPC sketch:
  Public subnets (2 AZs): ALB + IGW route
  Private subnets (2 AZs): EC2, NAT route out
  DB subnets: RDS, no internet route
  SG: ALB 443 from 0/0; EC2 from ALB; RDS from EC2

Layered like an onion.
example.walkthrough: Default-deny thinking wins: security groups deny all inbound by default — you open only what is needed. The exam's network questions reward the most restrictive correct option nearly every time.

pitfalls: Public subnets for databases — no isolation
NACL confused with security group — stateful vs stateless
NAT Gateway in a public subnet forgotten — private subnets stranded
lessons.try_it: Draw the 3-tier VPC: where do ALB, EC2, RDS live, and what routes do they get?

lessons.title: CloudFront and Route 53
concepts: CloudFront: global CDN — caches content at 400+ edge locations, cutting latency and origin load; integrates with S3, ALB, and EC2 origins
Route 53: managed DNS — domain registration, routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation), and health checks
Together: Route 53 routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint; CloudFront serves cached content from the nearest edge — the global-delivery pair
Exam signals: 'lowest latency worldwide' → CloudFront; 'DNS failover between regions' → Route 53 health checks + failover routing

example.code:
Global delivery:
  Static site, worldwide users -> S3 + CloudFront
  API, active-passive regions -> Route 53 failover routing
  A/B traffic split -> Route 53 weighted routing
  DDoS + WAF at edge -> CloudFront + Shield + WAF

Route, then cache.
example.walkthrough: CloudFront is not just caching: signed URLs/cookies (private content), origin failover, and edge functions (Lambda@Edge) make it a delivery platform. The exam usually tests the caching + origin story — know the rest as bonus.

pitfalls: CloudFront as 'just a cache' — miss the security/routing roles
Route 53 confused with a CDN
Single-region origin for a global audience with no CDN
lessons.try_it: Video streaming to 50 countries, some premium content: which services, and how is premium protected?

lessons.title: How AWS Pricing Works
concepts: Pay as you go: no long-term contracts for the base model — pay per second/hour/GB/request for what you consume
Pay less when you reserve: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances trade commitment for up to 72% off steady-state usage
Pay less per unit with volume: S3, data transfer, and many services tier down as usage grows — scale discounts are automatic
Pay less as AWS grows: 100+ price reductions historically — the exam wants 'AWS passes economies of scale to customers'

example.code:
Pricing levers:
  Commitment -> Savings Plans (steady workloads)
  Volume -> S3 tiers, transfer tiers (automatic)
  Timing -> Spot (interruptible), Off-peak patterns
  Growth -> AWS price cuts (historical trend)

Four ways the bill shrinks.
example.walkthrough: These four principles are exam canon — questions ask them nearly verbatim ('which pricing principle describes volume discounts?'). Memorize the exact four; they are free points.

pitfalls: Treating On-Demand as the only pricing
Missing that volume tiers are automatic
Forgetting the historical price-reduction trend
lessons.try_it: Your S3 bill dropped per-GB as data grew, with no action taken: which principle?

lessons.title: Free Tier, Cost Explorer, and Budgets
concepts: Free Tier: 12 months of limited EC2/S3/RDS + always-free Lambda/DynamoDB tiers — for learning and tiny workloads, with usage alerts essential
Cost Explorer: visualizes spend by service, account, and tag — with forecasting and rightsizing-adjacent insights
AWS Budgets: alerts (and actions) when spend or usage crosses thresholds — the guardrail against surprise bills
Exam trio: 'track and analyze spend' → Cost Explorer; 'get alerted on spend' → Budgets; 'learn AWS free' → Free Tier

example.code:
Billing toolkit:
  'Where did $5k go?' -> Cost Explorer
  'Tell me before we hit $10k' -> Budgets alert
  'Stop dev instances over budget' -> Budgets ACTIONS
  'Which team spent what?' -> Cost allocation tags

Question verb picks the tool.
example.walkthrough: Budgets ACTIONS (not just alerts) are the exam's depth: Budgets can actually stop EC2/RDS instances or apply SCPs when thresholds breach. 'Prevent overspend automatically' → Budgets with actions, not just an alert.

pitfalls: Cost Explorer confused with Budgets — analyze vs alert
Free Tier assumed unlimited — limits and expiry apply
No budget alerts — surprise bills are a choice
lessons.try_it: Finance wants an alert at 80% of budget and auto-stop of dev instances at 100%: which feature?

lessons.title: Consolidated Billing with Organizations
concepts: AWS Organizations: manage multiple accounts centrally — consolidated billing rolls all accounts into one payer bill
Volume discounts aggregate: usage across linked accounts pools into higher discount tiers — the whole org pays less per unit
Service Control Policies (SCPs): guardrails on what member accounts can do — e.g., deny leaving approved regions
Exam logic: 'single bill + pooled discounts + central control' → Organizations; SCPs are preventive guardrails, not grants of permission

example.code:
Organizations value:
  1 bill for 50 accounts -> consolidated billing
  Combined S3 usage -> deeper volume tier
  'No resources outside us-east-1' -> SCP
  Separate dev/prod blast radius -> separate accounts

Scale with control.
example.walkthrough: SCPs do not GRANT permissions — they only restrict what IAM policies could otherwise allow. The exam tests this negation explicitly: 'SCPs grant access' is always a wrong choice.

pitfalls: SCPs described as granting permissions — they only restrict
One account for everything — no blast-radius isolation
Missing the pooled volume-discount benefit
lessons.try_it: A company with 40 accounts wants one bill and a ban on non-US regions: which features?

lessons.title: Pricing Tools: Calculator and Compute Optimizer
concepts: AWS Pricing Calculator: estimate BEFORE you build — model architectures and compare regions, instance types, and commitment options
Compute Optimizer: ML-driven rightsizing recommendations for EC2, EBS, Lambda — 'you are over-provisioned' with evidence
Trusted Advisor cost checks: idle resources, unassociated EIPs, underutilized volumes — the waste finder (full checks need Business/Enterprise support)
Exam flow: estimate → Calculator; optimize existing → Compute Optimizer + Trusted Advisor; alert on future → Budgets

example.code:
Tool chain:
  Before: Pricing Calculator (what will it cost?)
  Now: Compute Optimizer (are we right-sized?)
  Waste: Trusted Advisor (what is idle?)
  Future: Budgets (alert me)

Each tool has its tense.
example.walkthrough: The exam loves the tense trick: 'estimate costs for a PLANNED architecture' → Pricing Calculator (not Cost Explorer, which analyzes PAST spend). Future = Calculator; past = Explorer.

pitfalls: Cost Explorer for pre-build estimates — wrong tense
Compute Optimizer confused with Trusted Advisor
Building first, pricing never
lessons.try_it: An architect must estimate a planned 3-tier build: which tool, and what two alternatives does the exam offer as distractors?

lessons.title: IAM: Users, Groups, Roles, Policies
concepts: Users: individual identities — for humans; Groups: collections of users sharing permissions; Roles: temporary credentials for apps and cross-account access
Policies: JSON documents granting/denying actions on resources — attach to users, groups, or roles; never hand-write what AWS managed policies cover
Roles over keys: applications assume roles (temporary credentials) — long-lived access keys are the leaked-credential incident waiting to happen
Exam hierarchy: humans → users in groups; applications → roles; permissions → policies; cross-account → roles with trust policies

example.code:
IAM setup:
  Devs -> 'Developers' group -> PowerUser-ish scoped policy
  CI/CD -> role (assumed, no stored keys)
  Partner account -> role + trust policy
  Break-glass -> admin user + MFA, MFA condition

Identity matches the actor.
example.walkthrough: The root account is radioactive: no access keys, MFA on, never daily use. The exam asks about root protection constantly — the answer is always lock it down maximally.

pitfalls: Access keys for applications — use roles
Permissions attached directly to users — use groups
Daily work as root — never
lessons.try_it: A CI pipeline needs S3 write access: user+key or role? Write the trust reasoning.

lessons.title: MFA, Least Privilege, and Credential Hygiene
concepts: MFA everywhere that matters: root, IAM users with console access, and privileged roles — the single highest-ROI security control
Least privilege: grant only the actions on only the resources needed — start narrow, expand on evidence, review with Access Analyzer
Credential hygiene: rotate keys, delete unused keys (90+ days), never commit secrets — use Secrets Manager/Parameter Store
Exam posture: given a choice, the MOST restrictive correct option wins — the Framework always prefers least privilege

example.code:
Hardening sprint:
  1. MFA on root + all console users
  2. Find unused keys (Credential Report) -> delete
  3. Access Analyzer: flag unused permissions -> trim
  4. Secrets out of code -> Secrets Manager

Restrictiveness is the default.
example.walkthrough: Access Analyzer's unused-access findings are the exam's 'how to enforce least privilege' answer: it identifies granted-but-unused permissions so you can trim them with evidence instead of guesses.

pitfalls: MFA 'later' — it is the first control, not the last
Admin* policies 'for simplicity' — the breach shortcut
Keys committed to repos — the #1 cloud breach pattern
lessons.try_it: An audit finds 12 unused access keys and 3 admin policies: what are the first three actions?

lessons.title: Encryption: KMS, TLS, and S3
concepts: Encryption at rest: EBS, S3, RDS, EFS all support it — enable by default; KMS manages the keys (AWS-managed or customer-managed CMKs)
Encryption in transit: TLS everywhere — CloudFront, ALB, and API endpoints terminate/originate TLS; never plaintext between tiers
KMS key types: AWS-managed (free, automatic rotation where supported) vs customer-managed CMKs (you control rotation, policies, and audit)
Exam mantra: 'protect data at rest and in transit' → KMS/TLS; 'control your own keys' → customer-managed CMK

example.code:
Encryption map:
  EBS volumes -> KMS at-rest (one checkbox)
  S3 objects -> SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS
  ALB -> ACM certificate, TLS listeners
  DB credentials -> Secrets Manager (KMS-backed)
  'We manage keys' -> CMK + rotation

Every layer, encrypted.
example.walkthrough: S3's default encryption now encrypts new objects automatically — but the exam still tests that YOU choose the key type and bucket policies. Defaults help; explicit configuration proves understanding.

pitfalls: Plaintext between app tiers 'inside the VPC' — encrypt in transit
One shared KMS key for everything, no rotation
Assuming encryption without verifying the configuration
lessons.try_it: A compliance rule demands customer-controlled key rotation for database encryption: which KMS key type?

lessons.title: Detection: CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty
concepts: CloudTrail: logs every API call — who did what, when, from where; the audit trail; enable in all regions, immutable storage
Config: records resource configuration history and evaluates rules ('are S3 buckets encrypted?') — compliance as continuous check
GuardDuty: ML threat detection on CloudTrail/VPC/DNS logs — finds compromised instances, crypto-mining, and unusual API patterns
Exam trio: 'who did what' → CloudTrail; 'is it configured right' → Config; 'is something malicious happening' → GuardDuty

example.code:
Detection stack:
  API audit trail -> CloudTrail (all regions)
  'S3 public?' continuous check -> Config rule
  Strange 3 AM API calls -> GuardDuty finding
  Central view -> Security Hub aggregates

Log, check, detect, aggregate.
example.walkthrough: The exam separates them by question verb: 'audit/track changes' = CloudTrail; 'ensure compliance over time' = Config; 'intelligent threat detection' = GuardDuty. Match the verb, get the point.

pitfalls: CloudTrail in one region only — attackers use others
Config confused with CloudTrail — history vs audit
GuardDuty expected to block — it DETECTS; WAF/NACLs block
lessons.try_it: An S3 bucket became public Tuesday; who changed it, and how do you prevent recurrence?

lessons.title: The Four Support Plans
concepts: Basic: free — 7 core Trusted Advisor checks, personal health dashboard, 24/7 customer service for billing (no technical support)
Developer: from $29/mo — business-hours email, <24h response on general guidance, for non-production experimenting
Business: from $100/mo — 24/7 phone/chat, <1h urgent response, FULL Trusted Advisor, IEM guidance
Enterprise On-Ramp ($5,500+/mo) and Enterprise ($15,000+/mo): <15-min critical response, TAM, Concierge team

example.code:
Plan ladder:
  Learning AWS -> Basic (free)
  Dev/test experiments -> Developer
  Production workloads -> Business (24/7, <1h)
  Critical + optimization -> Enterprise (TAM, <15min)

Production = Business minimum.
example.walkthrough: The exam's most-tested support fact: production workloads need Business (24/7 + 1-hour urgent). 'Cheapest plan for production with fast response' is ALWAYS Business, never Developer.

pitfalls: Developer plan for production — no 24/7, no urgent SLA
Basic expected to give technical support — billing only
Enterprise for a dev sandbox — massive overkill
lessons.try_it: A startup launches production Monday, needs <1h urgent response: which plan, and what is the monthly floor?

lessons.title: Trusted Advisor and Health Dashboard
concepts: Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks across cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits — FULL access needs Business/Enterprise; Basic/Developer get 7 core checks
Personal Health Dashboard: YOUR account's events — scheduled maintenance, outages affecting you; vs Service Health Dashboard: global AWS status
Exam distinction: 'is my account affected?' → Personal Health Dashboard; 'is AWS down?' → Service Health Dashboard
The 7 core checks include S3 bucket permissions, security groups, and IAM use — the free security baseline

example.code:
Dashboard decoder:
  'Is us-east-1 having issues?' -> Service Health
  'Is MY RDS affected by maintenance?' -> Personal Health
  'Am I wasting money?' -> Trusted Advisor (cost)
  'Are my SGs open?' -> Trusted Advisor (security)

Whose view is the question asking for?
example.walkthrough: Personal vs Service Health is a pure memorization pair that the exam tests directly. Mnemonic: PERSONAL = my account; SERVICE = AWS overall. One word in the stem decides it.

pitfalls: Full Trusted Advisor expected on Basic — 7 checks only
Service Health for account-specific maintenance
Ignoring the 7 free core checks
lessons.try_it: An exam stem says 'view events affecting your VPC maintenance': which dashboard?

lessons.title: TAM and the Concierge Team
concepts: Technical Account Manager (TAM): your named AWS guide — architecture reviews, escalation management, best-practice coaching (Enterprise plans)
Concierge team: billing and account specialists — cost optimization analysis, reserved-capacity planning (Enterprise)
Infrastructure Event Management (IEM): AWS engineers engaged for YOUR big events — launches, migrations, Prime Day-scale traffic (Business+ paid engagement, Enterprise included)
Exam mapping: 'named technical guide' → TAM; 'help with a major launch event' → IEM; 'billing optimization help' → Concierge

example.code:
Enterprise extras:
  Architecture guidance -> TAM
  Launch day engineers -> IEM engagement
  Bill analysis + RI planning -> Concierge
  15-min critical response -> Enterprise support

People, not just SLAs.
example.walkthrough: IEM is the sleeper exam topic: 'company expects 10x traffic for a product launch and wants AWS engineers involved' → Infrastructure Event Management. It is the only answer involving AWS staff at YOUR event.

pitfalls: TAM expected on Business plan — Enterprise only
IEM confused with regular support tickets
Concierge expected to write code — billing/account focus
lessons.try_it: A retailer expects 20x traffic on launch day and wants AWS engineers on standby: what do they engage?

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Plan
concepts: Decision tree: production? → Business minimum (24/7 + urgent SLA). Mission-critical + spend? → Enterprise (TAM, 15-min). Learning? → Basic. Pre-prod experiments? → Developer
Cost math: Business starts at $100/mo — trivial against one production outage; the exam frames it as insurance, not expense
Plan changes are flexible: upgrade before launches, downgrade after — support follows the business cycle
Exam trap: '24/7 technical support' as a requirement ELIMINATES Basic and Developer immediately — only Business and Enterprise qualify

example.code:
Chooser:
  Prod + 'fast response needed' -> Business
  Prod + 'dedicated guidance' -> Enterprise
  Staging experiments -> Developer
  Studying for CLF-C02 -> Basic
  Launch event -> Business + IEM engagement

Requirement filters the list.
example.walkthrough: When a scenario lists requirements, filter plans by elimination: 24/7 kills Basic/Developer; TAM kills Business; 'cheapest' + production = Business. The exam rarely requires finer discrimination than this.

pitfalls: Developer chosen for '24/7 phone support' — it has none
Enterprise for cost reasons alone — Business suffices
Forgetting plans can change with the business cycle
lessons.try_it: Filter: startup, production, needs 24/7 and full Trusted Advisor, $100/mo OK — which plan?

labs.title: Cloud value proposition — AWS CLI drill
labs.objective: Run a short sequence of AWS CLI commands that demonstrates cloud value proposition, then verify each result against the expected output.
steps: This lab reworks the Cloud Concepts practice scenario "The rack that shipped nothing" into commands you run yourself — same concept, hands-on instead of multiple choice.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: aws s3 ls — the listing names your lab buckets
Type exactly: aws sts get-caller-identity — the identity document includes your Account id
Type exactly: aws iam list-users — the user list carries the UserName field
In your own words, say what each command's output taught you about cloud value proposition.

foundations.why_needed: Cloud Practitioner is the cloud mental model: regions, services, billing, shared responsibility. Learn it here before the exam vocabulary.
VPCs, DNS, and HTTP underpin every AWS architecture question. Get the fundamentals first.

CLF-C02 is 65 multiple-choice and multiple-response questions in 90 minutes (roughly 80 seconds per question, passing score 700/1000). Answer what you know first and flag the rest: two choices are usually obviously wrong, leaving a 50/50 between concepts you can reason about. Beware absolutes like 'always', 'never', and 'zero downtime' — they are almost always the distractor. When two answers both sound right, pick the one that matches the shared responsibility model or the cheapest managed option; the exam rewards cloud-native thinking, not trivia.

simulations.title: Whose job is it anyway?
simulations.brief: A customer data leak is traced to a public S3 bucket. Three people are in the war room pointing fingers: the app team, the cloud team, and AWS. Walk the decision tree and assign responsibility correctly under the shared responsibility model.

steps.text: The bucket held customer exports and had a public ACL set by the app team's deploy script. Who owns the access control on customer data in S3?

choices.label: AWS — they own the S3 service
choices.feedback: AWS owns the S3 service itself (durability, availability), not your bucket policies.

choices.label: The customer (app team) — data access control is the customer's job
choices.feedback: Correct. Under the shared responsibility model, data classification and access control are always the customer's responsibility.

steps.text: Not quite — AWS secures the service, you secure your data in it. Try again: who owns the bucket ACL?

choices.label: The customer (app team)
choices.feedback: Right. The model is 'security OF the cloud' (AWS) vs 'security IN the cloud' (you).

steps.text: The leak also exposed that EC2 guest OS patching was 8 months behind. Who owns patching the guest OS?

choices.label: AWS — EC2 is their service
choices.feedback: Wrong: AWS patches the hypervisor and hardware. The guest OS inside your EC2 instance is your responsibility.

choices.label: The customer — guest OS patching is the customer's job
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the classic shared-responsibility exam trap: AWS manages the host, you manage the guest.

simulations.debrief: You applied the shared responsibility model to a realistic leak: AWS owns security OF the cloud, you own security IN the cloud — including your data, access controls, and guest OS.

sections.heading: Cloud Concepts
items: Cloud value proposition — the cloud's core value proposition is eliminating undifferentiated heavy lifting — racking, powering, cooling, and repairing physical infrastructure — so teams spend their time on the product.
Elasticity vs scalability — scalability covers growth; elasticity explicitly includes shrinking back down, which is what kills the idle-fleet waste.
CapEx to OpEx — trading fixed CapEx for variable OpEx means capacity becomes a pay-as-you-go utility expense, removing the upfront purchase and its approval bottleneck.

Serverless — lambda is serverless: it runs code in response to events, scales automatically from zero, bills per millisecond of execution, and requires no server patching.

IAM policies — S3 Block Public Access (account-level) acts as a guardrail that blocks public ACLs and policies regardless of individual bucket settings — prevention, not detection.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Cloud Concepts: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Shared Responsibility lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Core Services terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
